questions: Walk me through your approach to Two Sum — start with the brute force, then optimize.

answers: Brute force checks every pair, O(n²) time and O(1) space. To optimize, walk the array once and keep a hash map from value to index. For each element x, check whether target - x is already in the map before inserting x — this gives one pass, O(n) time and O(n) space, and correctly handles duplicates because you check before inserting the current element.

Sorting the whole frequency list is O(n log n) when you only need the top k. Instead, count frequencies with a hash map, then use a min-heap of size k: push elements and pop the smallest whenever the heap exceeds k. That's O(n log k), which is much better when k is small relative to n.

Sorting + two pointers is O(n log n) time but O(1) extra space (or O(n) if you must preserve original indices, since sorting loses them). The hash map approach is O(n) time but O(n) space. If you need the original indices and space isn't constrained, the hash map wins on time; if memory is tight and you don't need indices, sorting is a reasonable trade.

questions: How do you decide between two-pointer partitioning and a full merge sort for a 'sort this array' question?

answers: If the values fall into a small, known number of categories (e.g. two or three distinct groups like 0/1 or red/white/blue), a single-pass partitioning scheme with pointers gets O(n) time and O(1) space — that's the Dutch National Flag pattern. If the values are arbitrary and you need a general-purpose sort, you fall back to divide-and-conquer: split, recursively sort each half, and merge in linear time for O(n log n).

Maintain three pointers: low, mid, high. Everything before low is 0s, between low and mid is 1s, and after high is 2s; mid is the current element being examined. If arr[mid] is 0, swap with low and advance both low and mid. If it's 1, just advance mid. If it's 2, swap with high and decrement high without advancing mid, since the swapped-in value still needs examining. The loop ends when mid passes high.

The log n factor comes from recursively halving the array until subarrays have one element, which takes log n levels. At each level, merging all the subarrays back together touches every element once, so each level costs O(n), and log n levels gives O(n log n) total. The merge step itself is linear because you only ever advance through each of the two sorted halves once, comparing fronts and taking the smaller.

questions: What tells you a problem is a sliding window problem rather than, say, a two-pointer or prefix-sum problem?
In 'Minimum Window Substring', why do you expand the right pointer and shrink the left pointer, and what invariant do you maintain?

answers: The signal is usually 'longest' or 'shortest' contiguous subarray or substring satisfying some condition. If shrinking or growing a window from one side lets you incrementally maintain the condition — like a running count or a set of seen characters — that's sliding window. If you instead need a fixed relationship between two indices computed independently, that's more likely two pointers or prefix sum.

You expand the window by moving right until it contains all required characters, then shrink from the left as far as possible while it still satisfies that condition, recording the minimum length window seen. The invariant is a count map of required characters remaining to satisfy; expanding decreases the count, shrinking only proceeds while the count is fully satisfied.

Classic sliding window relies on the window's sum or count changing monotonically as you expand or shrink — negative numbers break that, since growing the window can decrease the sum. In that case, you typically switch to prefix sums combined with a hash map (to find complementary sums) or a different structure like a monotonic deque, rather than a simple two-pointer window.

questions: For 'Container With Most Water', why do you move the pointer at the shorter line inward rather than the taller one?
When do two pointers require the array to be sorted first, and when do they not?
What's the time complexity trade-off of two pointers on a sorted array versus a hash-map approach for pair-sum problems?
answers: The area is limited by the shorter of the two lines. If you move the pointer at the taller line inward, the width shrinks but the limiting height can only stay the same or get worse, so the area can't improve. Moving the shorter line's pointer is the only move that has a chance of finding a taller line and increasing the area, so it's the only move worth making.

Two pointers need sorting when you're exploiting order to decide which side to move — for example, in Two Sum on a sorted array, comparing the sum to the target tells you whether to move the left or right pointer inward. When pointers are just tracking positions for something like fast/slow cycle detection or in-place partitioning, order isn't required at all.

Two pointers on a pre-sorted array is O(n log n) if you have to sort first, then O(n) to scan, so O(n log n) overall, with O(1) extra space. The hash-map approach is O(n) time but O(n) space. If the array is already sorted, two pointers is strictly better; if it isn't and you can't destroy the original order, the hash map avoids the sort cost.

questions: Why does a prefix sum turn 'count subarrays with sum k' into a hash map lookup problem?
What edge case do people forget when initializing the prefix-sum frequency map?

answers: If prefix[i] is the sum of the first i elements, the sum of any subarray (i, j] equals prefix[j] - prefix[i]. So you're looking for pairs of prefix sums that differ by exactly k. As you scan and compute each prefix sum, you check how many times prefix[j] - k has already occurred, using a hash map of prefix-sum frequencies seen so far, which turns an O(n²) brute force into O(n).

You have to seed the map with prefix sum 0 occurring once before you start scanning, to account for subarrays that start from index 0 and already equal the target sum exactly. Forgetting that undercounts any subarray beginning at the very start of the array.

You precompute a 2D prefix sum where each cell holds the sum of the rectangle from the origin to that cell, built in O(rows × cols). Then any rectangular sub-rectangle sum can be computed in O(1) using inclusion-exclusion on four corner values, instead of resumming the rectangle every query. It's worth it whenever you have many range queries on a static grid.

questions: What invariant does a monotonic stack maintain, and what problem shape does that solve?
Walk through how a monotonic decreasing stack finds the next greater element for every array position.
How is 'Largest Rectangle in Histogram' related to monotonic stacks?
answers: A monotonic stack keeps its elements in strictly increasing or decreasing order by popping elements that violate that order as you push a new one. That's exactly the right tool for 'next greater/smaller element' style problems, because popping an element means you've just found its next greater (or smaller) neighbor — the current element you're pushing.

Scan left to right, and for each new value, pop everything on the stack smaller than it — each pop's next-greater answer is the current value, since it's the first larger element to its right. After popping, push the current value's index. Anything still on the stack at the end has no next greater element.

You keep a stack of indices with increasing bar heights. When you hit a bar shorter than the stack's top, that top bar can't extend any further right, so you pop it and compute the rectangle using its height and a width spanning from the new stack top to the current index. This finds, for every bar, the maximal rectangle where it's the shortest bar, in O(n) total.

questions: Binary search assumes a sorted array — how do you recognize a problem where it applies even though nothing looks explicitly sorted?

answers: The real requirement isn't a sorted array, it's a monotonic predicate — a yes/no answer that flips exactly once as you move along a range. If you can define 'is this candidate answer feasible' and that feasibility is monotonic in the candidate value, you can binary search on the answer itself, like minimizing the maximum load or finding a minimum capacity.

The usual bug is an infinite loop or missed element from inconsistent boundary updates — for example using mid = (lo+hi)/2 with hi = mid instead of hi = mid - 1 when you've already ruled out mid. The fix is to be explicit about whether your range is inclusive or half-open and keep the invariant consistent every iteration; a safe default is lo <= hi with hi = mid - 1 and lo = mid + 1 for a closed range.

At each step, at least one half of the array (from lo to mid, or mid to hi) is still properly sorted. Check which half is sorted by comparing arr[lo] to arr[mid], then check whether the target falls within that sorted half's range — if so recurse there, otherwise recurse into the other half. This keeps it O(log n) despite the rotation.

questions: What's the first step in nearly every interval-merging problem, and why does it matter so much?
How do you decide if two intervals overlap, and how do you merge them?

answers: Sort the intervals by start time. Once sorted, you only ever need to compare each interval to the last one you've kept, because any overlap must happen with the most recently added interval — you never have to look back further than that. Skipping the sort turns an O(n log n) problem into something that needs much more bookkeeping.

Two intervals [a,b] and [c,d], sorted so a <= c, overlap when c <= b. If they overlap, merge them into [a, max(b,d)]; if not, the first interval is finalized and you move on to comparing the next pair.

You're not merging overlapping meetings, you're counting the maximum number that are simultaneously in progress. Separate and sort all start times and end times independently; sweep through them in order, incrementing a room counter on a start and decrementing on an end when it happens before or at the next start. The maximum value the counter reaches is the answer. A min-heap of end times is an equivalent way to track this.

questions: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list without extra memory, and how do you then find where it begins?
Walk through reversing a singly linked list iteratively.
How is 'Copy List with Random Pointer' harder than a normal deep copy, and what's the O(1)-space trick?
answers: Floyd's cycle detection: a slow pointer moves one step, a fast pointer moves two; if there's a cycle they'll eventually meet inside it. To find the cycle's start, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time from there — they meet exactly at the cycle's entry point, because of the distance relationship between the head, the cycle start, and the meeting point.

Keep three pointers: prev starting at null, curr starting at head, and a temporary next. At each step, save next = curr.next, point curr.next back to prev, then advance prev = curr and curr = next. When curr is null, prev is the new head. It's O(n) time, O(1) space.

The random pointer can point anywhere in the list, including forward, so you can't build the copy in one pass with a simple hash map unless you accept O(n) extra space. The O(1)-space trick interleaves each cloned node right after its original (A→A'→B→B'→...), which lets you set each clone's random pointer as original.random.next, then unweave the interleaved list back into two separate lists.

questions: When would you reach for DFS over BFS on a tree or graph problem?
How do you handle a grid flood-fill / island-counting DFS without risking a stack overflow on very large grids?
For backtracking problems like generating permutations or subsets, what makes the difference between DFS and plain recursion explicit?
answers: DFS is the natural fit when you need to explore full paths before backtracking — counting paths, exploring all combinations, or when you need to process a subtree's results before its parent, like computing heights or validating a BST. BFS is better when you specifically need shortest-path-in-unweighted-graph or level-by-level structure.

Recursive DFS is clean but can blow the call stack on very large connected regions since many runtimes have shallow default recursion limits. An explicit stack (iterative DFS) avoids that risk while preserving the same visited-set logic — push neighbors instead of recursing, and pop until the stack is empty.

It's the same idea, but backtracking explicitly undoes a choice after exploring it — add a candidate to the current path, recurse, then remove it before trying the next candidate. That mutate-recurse-undo pattern is what lets you reuse one array/path structure across the whole search instead of allocating a new one at every level.

questions: Why is BFS the right tool for shortest path in an unweighted graph, but not in a weighted one?
Walk through multi-source BFS and give an example of when it's needed.
How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph using BFS, and how does that relate to topological sort?
answers: BFS explores nodes in increasing order of distance from the source because it processes the graph level by level using a queue — the first time you reach a node is guaranteed to be via a shortest path, but only when every edge has the same 'cost' of 1. With weighted edges, a longer path in terms of edge count can have a smaller total weight, so you need something like Dijkstra's that accounts for edge weight.

Instead of starting the queue with a single node, you seed it with every source node at distance 0 simultaneously, then run standard BFS. This correctly computes, for every cell, the shortest distance to the nearest of multiple sources at once — for example, 'Rotting Oranges,' where every already-rotten orange is a simultaneous source.

Kahn's algorithm: compute in-degrees for every node, start a BFS queue with all zero-in-degree nodes, and each time you process a node, decrement its neighbors' in-degrees, enqueuing any that hit zero. If you process fewer nodes than exist in the graph by the time the queue empties, there's a cycle, because some nodes never reached in-degree zero. If you process all nodes, the order you dequeued them in is a valid topological sort.

questions: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail on graphs with negative edge weights?
What data structure makes Dijkstra's algorithm efficient, and what's the resulting complexity?
How would you adapt Dijkstra to also reconstruct the actual shortest path, not just its length?
answers: Dijkstra greedily finalizes the shortest distance to a node as soon as it's popped from the priority queue, assuming no future relaxation could improve it — that assumption only holds if all remaining edge weights are non-negative. A negative edge could later reduce the distance to an already-finalized node, which Dijkstra would miss. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights by relaxing every edge repeatedly instead of greedily finalizing.

A min-heap (priority queue) keyed on current best-known distance, so you always expand the closest unvisited node next. With a binary heap, that gives O((V + E) log V) time — each edge can trigger a heap insertion, and each is O(log V).

Keep a parent/predecessor array alongside the distance array; whenever you relax an edge and improve a node's distance, record the node you relaxed it from. Once the algorithm finishes, walk backward from the destination through the parent pointers to reconstruct the path, then reverse it.

questions: What do path compression and union by rank/size each contribute to Union-Find's efficiency?
Why is Union-Find the natural structure for 'number of connected components' or 'redundant connection' problems?
Walk through Kruskal's algorithm for minimum spanning tree and explain where Union-Find comes in.
answers: Path compression flattens the tree during find operations by pointing nodes directly to the root, so future lookups are faster. Union by rank/size attaches the smaller tree under the bigger one's root during union, preventing the tree from growing tall in the first place. Together they give near-constant amortized time per operation — technically O(α(n)), the inverse Ackermann function.

Those problems are fundamentally asking whether two nodes already belong to the same group, and merging groups as you process edges — exactly what union and find operations do. You process each edge once: if the two endpoints are already connected, that edge is redundant (or would create a cycle); otherwise, you union them.

Sort all edges by weight ascending. Go through them in order, and for each edge, use Union-Find to check if its two endpoints are already connected — if not, add the edge to the MST and union the two sets; if they are already connected, adding it would create a cycle, so skip it. You stop once you've added n-1 edges for n nodes.

questions: How do you tell whether a problem actually has the greedy-choice property, versus needing DP?
For 'Jump Game II' (minimum jumps to reach the end), what's the greedy insight?
In interval scheduling — maximizing the number of non-overlapping intervals you can select — why does sorting by end time (not start time) give the greedy optimum?
answers: You need to be able to argue that a locally optimal choice at each step never precludes reaching a globally optimal solution — usually via an exchange argument, showing that any optimal solution can be transformed into one that includes your greedy choice without getting worse. If the optimal choice at a step depends on what you choose later, or overlapping subproblems interact, that's a sign you need DP instead.

Track the farthest index reachable from the current 'jump window,' and the end of the current window. As you scan, keep extending the farthest reachable index; once you reach the end of the current window, you must take a jump, so increment the jump count and extend the window to the farthest index found so far. This greedily commits to a jump only when forced to, which minimizes total jumps.

Sorting by end time and always picking the interval that finishes earliest among those still compatible leaves the most room for future intervals. Sorting by start time doesn't have that guarantee, because an early-starting interval can still block out a lot of the timeline if it runs long. The exchange argument shows any optimal solution can be rearranged to match this earliest-finish-first choice without losing intervals.

questions: What's the time complexity advantage a trie gives you over a hash set of strings for prefix queries?
How is a trie node typically structured, and how do you mark the end of a word?
When would a trie be the wrong choice compared to a simpler hash set, even for prefix problems?
answers: A hash set can tell you if an exact string exists in O(1) average, but checking whether any string starts with a given prefix requires scanning every entry, O(n · L) in the worst case. A trie answers 'does any word start with this prefix' in O(L) time, where L is the prefix length, by just walking down L trie nodes, regardless of how many words are stored.

Each node holds an array or map of children keyed by character, plus a boolean flag (often isEndOfWord) marking whether a valid word ends at that node. Insertion walks character by character, creating child nodes as needed, and sets that flag true at the final character's node.

If you never actually need prefix queries — only exact membership checks — a trie adds memory overhead (a node per character, potentially with a full alphabet-sized children array) for no benefit over a hash set's O(1) average lookup. Tries earn their keep specifically when prefix matching, autocomplete, or word-with-wildcard search is part of the requirement.

questions: 'Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)' asks for average O(1) insert, delete, and random access all at once — why doesn't a plain hash set or array alone satisfy that?
When would you reach for a heap versus a balanced BST when you need ordered access to a dynamic set?
What's the core design idea behind an LRU cache, and which two structures does it combine?
answers: An array alone gives O(1) random access via a random index, but deletion from the middle is O(n) if you shift elements. A hash set alone gives O(1) insert/delete/lookup but has no way to pick a uniformly random element in O(1). The trick is combining both: an array for O(1) random-index access, plus a hash map from value to its array index for O(1) lookup, and on deletion, swap the target with the last array element before popping, updating the map, to avoid shifting.

A heap gives you O(log n) insert and O(log n) extract-min/max, but only efficient access to the single min or max — no efficient arbitrary rank or range queries. A balanced BST (or a language's ordered map/set) supports O(log n) insert, delete, and lookup of arbitrary elements, plus in-order traversal and range queries. If you only ever need the extreme element, a heap is simpler and often faster in practice; if you need general ordered access, use a BST-backed structure.

You need O(1) get and put while always knowing which entry was least recently used. A hash map gives O(1) lookup from key to a node, and a doubly linked list maintains usage order — moving a node to the front on every access, and evicting from the back when the cache is full. The combination gives O(1) for both operations, which neither structure alone would provide.

questions: A camera works in daylight but fails at night. What changed in the input, and what can software recover?
Why can a 2×2 matrix not represent translation, and how do homogeneous coordinates fix it?
Why does averaging N frames reduce noise, and when does it fail?
What is aliasing, and how do you prevent it when downsampling?
What is an image pyramid used for?
A model trained in PyTorch performs badly when served with OpenCV image loading. What do you check first?
Can gamma correction or histogram equalization recover detail in blown-out highlights?
Which filter would you use for salt-and-pepper noise, and is it also best for Gaussian sensor noise?
How does a bilateral filter differ from a Gaussian filter?
Why is deblurring ill-posed, and how is it stabilized?
answers: Fewer photons mean more shot noise, higher gain amplifies it, longer exposure adds motion blur, and lighting shifts color. Software can denoise and adjust contrast, but it cannot recover detail that was never captured; that needs better capture or night training data.

A 2×2 matrix always maps the origin to itself, so translation is not linear. Writing points as (x, y, 1) lets a 3×3 matrix express translation, rotation, scale, and perspective, and lets transforms compose by matrix multiplication.
Independent zero-mean noise has variance reduced by 1/N (standard deviation by 1/√N). It fails for shared errors such as fixed-pattern noise or bias, and for moving objects, which ghost or blur.

Detail finer than the new grid can represent folds into false low-frequency patterns such as moiré. Low-pass filter (blur or area interpolation) before subsampling so that detail is removed instead of misrepresented.
It stores the same image at several resolutions, enabling coarse-to-fine search, multi-scale detection, and cheaper processing of large structures.
Channel order: OpenCV loads BGR while most training pipelines use RGB. Then check numeric scaling and normalization, layout (HWC vs CHW), and resize interpolation.
No. Clipped pixels all saturate to the same value, so the information is gone. Intensity transforms only remap existing values; recovery requires capture changes such as exposure control or HDR.

A median filter: isolated outliers do not move the median and edges are preserved. For Gaussian noise, weighted averaging (Gaussian or bilateral) is usually better because every sample carries useful information.
It weights neighbors by both spatial distance and intensity similarity, so it smooths within regions while preserving edges. The cost is more computation and possible flat, cartoon-like regions.

Blur suppresses high frequencies, so inverting it amplifies noise wherever the signal is weak. Stabilize with an accurate blur-kernel estimate plus regularization or priors such as Wiener filtering, total variation, or learned priors.

questions: Why smooth an image before computing gradients for edge detection?
Walk through the Canny edge detector.
What do morphological opening and closing do?
Why are corners better features to match than points on an edge?
Why are nearest-neighbor descriptor matches not enough to align two images?
How does RANSAC work, and what drives the number of iterations?
When is a single homography a valid model between two views?
What are intrinsics and extrinsics, and what happens to them if you resize the image by half?
Why is stereo depth unreliable for distant objects?
What is the aperture problem in optical flow, and how do methods handle it?
answers: Differentiation amplifies high-frequency noise. Smoothing (as in Sobel or derivative-of-Gaussian) suppresses it; a larger smoothing scale gives fewer spurious edges but loses fine, precisely localized ones.

Gaussian smoothing, gradient magnitude and direction, non-maximum suppression to thin edges to one pixel, then hysteresis with two thresholds: keep strong edges and weak edges connected to strong ones.
Opening (erode then dilate) removes small specks and thin protrusions; closing (dilate then erode) fills small holes and gaps. Both roughly preserve the size of larger shapes.

A corner changes intensity in two directions, so its position is fixed in 2D; along an edge, position is ambiguous. Harris detects this via the structure tensor: both eigenvalues large means a corner.
Repeated textures and noise create confident wrong matches. Filter with the ratio test or mutual matching, then verify geometrically by fitting a transformation with RANSAC and counting inliers.

Repeatedly sample a minimal set (4 pairs for a homography), fit a model, count inliers within a threshold, keep the best, and refit on its inliers. Iterations grow with the outlier ratio and the sample size: N = log(1−p) / log(1−wˢ).
When the scene is planar or the camera only rotates. A translating camera viewing objects at different depths creates parallax that no single homography can align.

Extrinsics are the camera's rotation and translation; intrinsics are focal lengths and the principal point. Halving the image halves fx, fy, cx, cy; cropping shifts the principal point; extrinsics are unchanged.

Depth is Z = f·B / d, so depth error grows roughly with Z² for a fixed disparity error. Far objects have tiny disparities, where a one-pixel mismatch is a large depth error; a wider baseline, longer focal length, or subpixel matching help.

Brightness constancy gives one equation (Iₓu + I_yv + I_t = 0) for two unknowns, so motion along an edge is invisible locally. Lucas–Kanade pools a textured window, Horn–Schunck adds smoothness, and coarse-to-fine pyramids handle large motions.

questions: A video-frame classifier scores 99% on a random split but fails on new videos. Why?
Why does a neural network need nonlinear activations?
When do you use softmax versus independent sigmoids at the output?
Why pass raw logits to a cross-entropy loss instead of applying softmax first?
What is the gradient of softmax cross-entropy with respect to the logits?
How is the gradient computed for a convolution weight shared across all positions?
What do loss.backward() and optimizer.step() each do, and why call zero_grad()?
How does AdamW differ from Adam with L2 regularization?
You increase batch size and learning rate together and the loss starts oscillating. What do you check?
Training accuracy is excellent but validation is poor. What do you prioritize?
answers: Leakage: near-duplicate frames from the same video landed in both train and test. Split by group (video, camera, site, or time) so evaluation matches deployment.
A stack of linear layers collapses into one linear map. Nonlinearities such as ReLU let the network represent complex functions; ReLU is also cheap and does not saturate for positive inputs.
Softmax for mutually exclusive classes (probabilities sum to one); independent sigmoids for multi-label tasks where several labels can be true at once.
The loss computes log-softmax internally with the log-sum-exp trick for numerical stability. Applying softmax first double-applies it and can underflow and distort gradients.
p − y: predicted probabilities minus the one-hot target. It is bounded and simple, which is why softmax and cross-entropy pair so well.
It is the sum of the contributions from every position where the weight is used. The gradient always has the same shape as the parameter.
backward computes gradients and adds them to .grad; step updates the weights. Gradients accumulate by default, so they must be cleared every iteration unless you accumulate on purpose.

With Adam + L2 the penalty enters the gradient and is rescaled by the adaptive denominator, weakening it for some weights. AdamW decouples weight decay and shrinks weights directly, giving more consistent regularization.

Larger batches reduce gradient noise and allow a higher learning rate, often scaled roughly linearly, but only with warmup and within limits. Inspect loss curves and gradient norms; lower the learning rate or add warmup before changing anything else.

First rule out leakage, split mismatch, and label problems. Then add data or augmentation, regularize (weight decay, dropout, label smoothing), use early stopping, or start from a pretrained backbone, guided by learning curves.

questions: Compare the parameter counts of a standard 3×3 convolution and a depthwise-separable one for 256 → 256 channels.
What is the difference between translation equivariance and invariance in CNNs?
What is the formula for a convolution's output size?
What is the receptive field of two 3×3 convolutions where the first has stride 2?
Why can adding layers to a plain network increase training error, and how do residual connections fix it?
What problem does a Feature Pyramid Network solve?
Why is BatchNorm a poor choice at batch size 1–2, and what do you use instead?
A model's predictions change depending on what else is in the batch at inference. What is the likely bug?
Which augmentations would you reject for reading text or for left-versus-right anatomy?
You have 500 labeled images from a new camera. How do you choose a fine-tuning strategy?
answers: Standard: 3·3·256·256 ≈ 590K. Depthwise-separable: 3·3·256 + 256·256 ≈ 68K, about 8.7× fewer. It assumes spatial filtering and channel mixing can be factored apart.
Convolution is equivariant: shifting the input shifts the feature map. Pooling and global pooling add approximate invariance. Stride and padding break exact equivariance.
floor((W + 2P − K) / S) + 1. For example, 224 input, kernel 3, padding 1, stride 2 gives 112.
7. Each layer adds (k−1) × the product of earlier strides: 1 + 2·1 + 2·2 = 7. Stacking small kernels reaches large receptive fields with fewer parameters and more nonlinearity.
It is an optimization problem, not overfitting: deep plain stacks struggle to even learn the identity. y = x + F(x) makes the identity easy (F = 0) and gives gradients a direct path.

Deep features are semantically strong but low-resolution, and shallow ones the reverse. FPN's top-down path with lateral connections gives strong semantics at every scale, which especially helps small objects.
Batch statistics become noisy or degenerate, and they mismatch the running statistics used at evaluation. Use GroupNorm or LayerNorm (per-example statistics), or freeze pretrained BatchNorm.
The model was left in training mode, so BatchNorm uses batch statistics (and dropout is active). Call model.eval() to use running statistics.
Horizontal flips (mirrored text, swapped sides) and large rotations for text. An augmentation must preserve the label, and geometric augmentations must also transform boxes, masks, and keypoints.

Start from a pretrained backbone: run a linear probe as a baseline, then fine-tune the top layers or the whole network with a low learning rate, strong augmentation, and early stopping on new-camera validation data. Go deeper only if the probe underfits.

questions: A defect classifier has 99% accuracy but misses most defects. What went wrong?
Define IoU and explain NMS, including when NMS fails.
Compare one-stage and two-stage detectors.
AP at IoU 0.5 is strong but AP at 0.75 is poor. What does that tell you?
How is COCO-style mAP computed?
Why can a segmentation model have high pixel accuracy but useless masks?
Distinguish semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation.
What problem does CTC loss solve in OCR?
How do you train and evaluate visual embeddings for retrieval?
Two similar people cross behind an obstacle. How do you reduce identity switches?
answers: With 1% defects, predicting 'no defect' scores 99%. Use precision, recall, and the PR curve; pick the threshold from the cost of misses versus false alarms; consider class weighting, focal loss, or resampling.

IoU = area of overlap / area of union. NMS keeps the highest-scoring box and removes others above an IoU threshold, repeating. In crowded scenes it suppresses real overlapping objects; use Soft-NMS or set-based detectors such as DETR.

Two-stage (Faster R-CNN) proposes regions then refines them: more accurate on small and crowded objects but slower. One-stage (YOLO, RetinaNet) predicts densely in one pass: faster, and focal loss addresses its extreme foreground–background imbalance.
The model finds objects but localizes boxes loosely. Improve box regression (for example a GIoU loss, higher-resolution features, or a refinement stage) and check box-label consistency.

Per class, rank detections by score and match each to an unmatched ground truth at IoU ≥ threshold (TP, else FP), then take the area under the precision–recall curve. Average over classes and IoU thresholds 0.5 to 0.95.

Background dominates the pixels, so predicting background everywhere scores well. Use per-class IoU or Dice, train with Dice or focal loss for imbalance, and use skip connections (U-Net) to recover fine boundaries.

Semantic: a class per pixel with no identities. Instance: a separate mask per countable object. Panoptic: every pixel gets a class, plus an instance ID for 'things' (people, cars) but not 'stuff' (road, sky); it is scored with Panoptic Quality.

It trains sequence recognition without per-character alignment: the model outputs a distribution per time step including a blank, and CTC sums over every alignment that collapses to the target. Evaluate with character and word error rates plus exact field match.

Use metric learning (contrastive, triplet, or InfoNCE loss) with positives defined by the task's relevance rule (same SKU, not just similar look) and hard negatives. Evaluate recall@K on held-out queries, and measure approximate-index recall separately from embedding quality.

Combine a motion model (Kalman filter) with appearance embeddings for association (as in DeepSORT), match with the Hungarian algorithm, and keep lost tracks alive briefly for re-identification. Measure ID switches, IDF1, or HOTA separately from detection quality.

questions: Write scaled dot-product attention and give the shapes for a batch of image tokens.
How does a Vision Transformer turn an image into tokens?
What happens to compute if you halve the ViT patch size?
Would you choose a CNN or a ViT for a small dataset?
How does contrastive self-supervised learning (SimCLR) work?

answers: softmax(QKᵀ / √dₖ)V. For B images, N tokens, d dims: Q, K, V are B×N×d (per head B×h×N×dₕ), the weights are B×h×N×N, and the output is B×N×d. Dividing by √dₖ keeps logits from saturating the softmax.

Split it into P×P patches, flatten and linearly project each one (equivalent to a stride-P convolution), add position embeddings, and optionally prepend a class token. A 224×224 image with 16×16 patches gives 196 tokens.
4× more tokens and about 16× more attention pairs, because attention is quadratic in token count. Windowed and hierarchical designs such as Swin keep cost roughly linear in image size.

A CNN's locality and translation equivariance make it data-efficient. A ViT needs large-scale pretraining or strong augmentation and distillation (DeiT); with a good pretrained ViT, fine-tuning can win. Compare both on a held-out set under the same budget.

Two augmented views of one image are positives and other images in the batch are negatives, trained with the InfoNCE loss. The augmentations define which invariances are learned, and it benefits from many negatives.

Every input maps to the same embedding, trivially satisfying 'make views agree.' It is prevented with negatives (contrastive), a stop-gradient with a momentum teacher plus centering (BYOL, DINO), variance–covariance penalties (VICReg), or reconstruction targets (MAE).

It masks about 75% of patches; the encoder sees only the visible ones (cheap), and a light decoder reconstructs the masked pixels. The high ratio keeps the task hard because images are redundant. Judge it by linear probing and fine-tuning.

Image and text encoders are trained contrastively so matching image–caption pairs score high cosine similarity. To classify, embed prompts like 'a photo of a {class}' and pick the one most similar to the image.

The domain may be far from web pretraining (medical, industrial), results are sensitive to prompt wording, class names can be rare or ambiguous, and fine-grained differences may not be captured. Mitigate with prompt ensembles, a few-shot linear probe, or fine-tuning.

A heavy image encoder runs once per image (cacheable); a light prompt encoder and mask decoder run per point or box prompt and return several candidate masks. Adapt it by measuring mask IoU on labeled domain samples, then fine-tune the decoder or adapters, and track annotation time saved.

questions: Annotators disagree about faint defects. How do you fix the data before training?
The model works in a notebook but deployed boxes are shifted. What do you investigate?
What sanity checks do you run before a full training run?
A new detector cannot beat the baseline. What do you check before trying a bigger backbone?
What is calibration, and how do you measure and fix it?
Overall AP improves but night-time performance worsens. Do you ship?
Distinguish covariate shift, label shift, and concept shift.
A factory changes cameras and false alarms rise. How do you diagnose it?
A model takes 20 ms on the GPU but requests take 150 ms. How do you find the bottleneck?
Compare quantization, distillation, and pruning for faster inference.
answers: Write a guideline with edge-case examples (faint, occluded, truncated), measure inter-annotator agreement, adjudicate disagreements, consider an explicit 'ambiguous' label, and keep a re-labeled gold set for evaluation.

Train–serve preprocessing skew: resize or letterbox padding not reversed, aspect ratio, EXIF orientation, RGB/BGR, normalization, and box format (xyxy vs xywh, normalized vs pixels). Run one image through both pipelines and diff the tensors.
Overfit one small batch to near-zero loss, visualize augmented inputs with labels drawn on them, and confirm the initial loss is about ln(C) for C classes.

Verify labels and preprocessing, tune the learning rate and schedule, confirm both use the same evaluation protocol, ablate one change at a time, and slice errors (small objects, rare classes). Scale up only if the model is underfitting.

Confidence should match observed accuracy. Measure with reliability diagrams and Expected Calibration Error; fix with temperature scaling on a validation set, which does not change ranking or accuracy.

Weigh the slice's importance (safety, traffic share), check that the drop is statistically real, and apply per-slice guardrails. Do not ship if a critical slice regresses past tolerance; collect night data or gate the rollout.

Covariate: P(x) changes (new camera, lighting) but P(y|x) holds. Label: P(y) changes (defect rate). Concept: P(y|x) changes (new defect definition). Input drift monitoring flags change, but labeled samples are needed to confirm an accuracy drop.

First rule out pipeline mismatch: resolution, color, exposure, compression, and orientation; compare input statistics and inspect samples. If it is a real domain shift, label new-camera data, fine-tune, augment for camera variation, and recalibrate the threshold.

Profile end to end: network transfer, image decoding, CPU preprocessing, queueing or batching waits, host–device copies, postprocessing such as NMS, and serialization. Fix the largest stage, for example with GPU preprocessing, pipelining, or tuned batching.

Quantization (FP32 → INT8) gives about 4× smaller weights and speedups on supported hardware, with QAT if accuracy drops. Distillation trains a smaller student on teacher outputs. Structured pruning yields real speedups; unstructured needs sparse kernels. Re-check accuracy per slice after each.

questions: A support model recognizes the cancellation intent in “cancel that.” What else must be established before an order can be canceled?
Two intent models both classify 90 of 100 messages correctly. What evidence would let you choose between them?
A random message split beats a conversation-grouped time split by 19 accuracy points. What leakage and availability checks come before model redesign?
answers: The system needs the intended order, enough conversation context, authorization, and an action policy. If the referent remains ambiguous, ask for clarification or review. Intent accuracy measures one stage; it does not establish that executing the action is correct.

Inspect which ten messages each misses, per-intent support, costly confusions, and their deployed routing or review policies. Compare latency and uncertainty on representative data. The same accuracy can conceal very different wrongful-action and missed-request costs.

Inspect shared conversations, duplicated templates, related documents, and features written after the original decision time. Check label-policy and traffic changes too. Rebuild the evaluation to match the intended deployment; the score difference suggests hypotheses but does not prove one cause.

questions: A language model gives “cats,” then “sleep,” then END conditional probabilities 0.4, 0.5, and 0.8. What is the sequence probability, and what if the final factor is zero?
You annotate only cases selected by model uncertainty, then report accuracy on that same pool. Why is that not a representative deployment estimate?
A query vector is [1,0], with document vectors [1,1] and [2,2]. Compare their dot products and cosine similarities, and explain the ranking implication.
A phrase occurs in 80% of spam and 5% of legitimate messages, while spam is 1% of traffic. Estimate spam risk for a phrase-bearing message.
The true two-class distribution is [0.5,0.5], but the model predicts [0.9,0.1]. Is the true entropy equal to cross-entropy? Use natural logs.
answers: Multiplying the chain-rule factors gives 0.16. A zero factor makes the complete sequence probability zero even if earlier tokens are likely. Inspect smoothing, vocabulary, and termination behavior rather than treating fluent local predictions as proof of a well-scored sequence.

The selection policy changes which examples receive labels and often overrepresents difficult cases while missing confident mistakes. Keep independent representative audits or an appropriately designed evaluation sample. Targeted active-learning data can help training without becoming an unbiased test of traffic quality.

The dot products are 1 and 2. Both cosine similarities are 1/√2, about 0.707. Doubling a document vector changes its magnitude but not direction, so dot-product ranking can reward a length difference that cosine removes. Choose the scoring geometry that matches training and relevance.

The spam-and-phrase probability is 0.008; legitimate-and-phrase probability is 0.0495. Bayes’ rule gives 0.008/0.0575, about 13.9%. The phrase is strong relative evidence, but legitimate traffic is much more common. Reversing the conditional without the base rate would exaggerate risk.

True entropy is about 0.693 nats. Cross-entropy is −0.5 log 0.9 −0.5 log 0.1, about 1.204. Their difference, about 0.511, is the directed KL mismatch. The model is more confident than the evidence supports; its own low entropy is not a quality guarantee.

questions: A cleaning pipeline changes “I do not recommend it” into “recommend.” Why can a larger sentiment model fail to repair the result?
A name detector predicts the right processed-text span but highlights the wrong characters after an emoji. What would you inspect?
A toy tokenizer starts with l, o, w, e, r and applies frozen merges l+o, lo+w, then e+r. What sequence remains, and does inference learn new merges from this request?
An unseen surname becomes six subword tokens. How do you decide whether to change the tokenizer?
Using count × (1 + log((N+1)/(df+1))), compare a term appearing twice in one of three fitting documents with one appearing twice in all three. What does the difference mean?
A bag-of-words baseline confuses “dog bites man” with “man bites dog.” You can afford more lexical features and must preserve exact product codes. What would you test, and what limits remain?

Can a highly accurate cross-encoder reranker fix supporting documents absent from the first-stage candidate set?
What is an important risk of directly adding raw BM25 scores and cosine similarities?
A cited page is topically relevant but does not state the claimed deadline. What should evidence-only evaluation record?
Why is an oracle-context experiment useful when debugging incorrect grounded answers?
answers: Retrieval supplies evidence in the current input context. It does not normally execute an optimizer update on model parameters. Later requests need their own evidence access, unless another explicit training or persistence mechanism has been introduced.

Inspect structural boundaries, metadata, and whether each retrieved unit preserves the applicable condition. Test complete answerability of returned chunks and consider coherent structural grouping or neighboring context. A larger embedding alone cannot restore omitted text.

Exact identifiers may be rare or poorly represented in learned vector geometry while remaining easy lexical matches. Compare lexical, dense, and hybrid results on identifier slices. Aggregate semantic-query quality does not guarantee code lookup accuracy.

The ANN approximation or its settings are implicated before the encoder. Inspect index construction, search effort, filtering, and recall against exact search. If exact search also failed, embeddings, chunking, or query formulation would become stronger candidates.

No. A reranker scores only candidates it receives. Improve candidate coverage, ingestion, or access filtering first, and measure relevant-document presence before reranking separately from its final rank.

Their scales and distributions need not be comparable, so one source may dominate arbitrarily. Calibrate a combination on held-out relevance judgments or use a defined rank-fusion method. Evaluate complementary coverage and downstream answer quality.

It should record an unsupported claim and an inaccurate supporting citation even if the deadline happens to be true elsewhere. Check support at the claim and source-version level, not merely whether the cited document concerns the topic.

Supplying ideal evidence isolates the generator and prompt from retrieval errors. If answers improve strongly, retrieval or context selection is likely a bottleneck. The oracle result is diagnostic and does not itself represent achievable production retrieval.

questions: A model is selected after repeatedly checking the same final test set. Why does the reported score become optimistic?
Average natural-log token loss is log(5). What is perplexity, and which comparison conditions matter?
A longer answer beats a short correct answer under one model judge. How would you investigate the judging behavior?

A retrieved page contains an instruction to send all customer records to a new destination. Which layer must reject unauthorized execution?
A model refuses every request in a harmful-output test and earns a perfect safety score. Why is that incomplete?
A privacy review deletes sensitive source documents. Why should it still inspect model outputs, caches, and logs?
answers: The test set has become a source of selection feedback, making it function more like validation. Keep a genuinely held-out set for fixed choices and account for repeated comparisons. Group related examples so leakage does not compound the selection bias.

Perplexity is five. It is meaningful for models evaluated on compatible token units, data, and masking conventions. It does not independently measure factual correctness or instruction-following, and raw values across different tokenizers should not be compared directly.

Hold correctness and useful content constant while varying length, reverse candidate order, hide model identities, and compare expert human decisions. Inspect rubric specificity and verbosity bias rather than assuming the longer answer contains better reasoning.

It can be faithful to the supplied document but incorrect under a current-policy truth standard. Record source freshness and authority separately, and evaluate whether retrieval supplied the appropriate version. One combined score would hide the failure stage.

Diversity and coverage are missing. Review a sufficiently representative sample set, compare distribution statistics under controlled preprocessing, and inspect requested attributes. Attractive selected samples cannot establish broad generative quality or absence of memorization.

An independent executor or authorization layer must enforce the requester's actual permissions and allowed destinations. The retrieved text is untrusted evidence, not authority. Prompting can help interpretation but cannot replace the permission boundary.

The test omits allowed requests and therefore cannot measure over-refusal or usefulness. Evaluate harmful-request handling alongside legitimate task completion across relevant languages and groups. Refusal alone is not a complete safety objective.

Learned weights may retain training-specific information, and copies can persist in prompts, retrieval indexes, caches, or logs. Source deletion does not automatically remove these paths. Verify the system's actual data handling rather than promising exact removal without evidence.

The estimate is 2×16×2×1024×4×64×2=33554432 bytes, or 32 MiB. The leading two counts keys and values. Actual deployment also needs weights, workspace, temporary activations, and allocation overhead.

It tiles and reorganizes the exact attention operation to reduce slow-memory traffic and avoid materializing the full score matrix. Full pairwise score work still scales quadratically for a full sequence, although practical runtime and memory use can improve substantially.

Its completed slot can accept new work while other sequences continue. This reduces idle slots but requires scheduling memory and compute across requests. Throughput improvements must be assessed alongside first-token delay, tail latency, and prefill interference.

Acceptance is min(1,0.2/0.5)=0.4. Rejected proposals require sampling from the normalized positive target-minus-draft residual distribution. Accepting every sufficiently likely token or resampling arbitrarily would generally alter the target distribution.

Not safely by text equality alone. Cache identity must include compatible model and adapter versions, tokenization, formatting, positions, and authorization boundaries. Hidden states computed under different parameters need not represent the new model's prefix.

Compare cost per successful complete request, including prompts, outputs, retrieval, tools, verification, retries, and failures. Evaluate matched quality and latency requirements on representative traffic. A per-token price or isolated throughput figure is insufficient.

answers: No. Reading context during ordinary inference changes the available input, not stored parameters. A training update would require an objective, gradient computation, and optimizer update.
0.12 by the probability chain rule. Multiplying marginal token frequencies instead would incorrectly discard the dependence on the prefix.
[8,20,64]. Token IDs choose rows from the 1000-row table; each position receives a 64-dimensional vector.
The probabilities are [0.5,0.25,0.25]. Negative log target probability is log 2, approximately 0.693. Cross-entropy implementations generally receive raw logits rather than these probabilities.
Substitution gives W2(W1x+b1)+b2=(W2W1)x+(W2b1+b2). Nonlinear activations prevent this collapse and enable richer input-dependent transformations.
The new weight is 1−0.05×4=0.8. Backpropagation computes the derivative; the optimizer applies the update. The local derivative does not guarantee a finite large step improves loss.
Their dot product is 2, while cosine is 1 because they point in the same direction. Dot-product scoring can be affected by vector norms; cosine normalizes those norms for nonzero vectors.
KL(p||q)=log 2. The reverse divergence is infinite because q assigns positive mass to the second token where p assigns zero. KL is directional and its support requirements matter.

What remains unchanged if RoPE rotates fixed query and key vectors by the same additional angle?

Loss masking controls which predictions contribute to the objective. Attention masking controls information access. A visible future token can leak its information even when its own target loss is ignored.

Their dot product is unchanged because the relative rotation is unchanged. The relative positional gap, rather than the shared absolute shift, determines that pair’s positional contribution under the stated fixed-content comparison.
LayerNorm subtracts the mean 2 and divides by standard deviation 1, producing [−1,1]. RMSNorm divides by sqrt(5) without mean subtraction, producing approximately [0.447,1.342].

The full source is available conditioning information, accessed through cross-attention. Future target tokens are unknown at generation and must remain hidden during target-side self-attention training.
Stored expert weights total four million parameters; two million expert parameters are activated per token before shared layers. A batch may use all experts, and routing communication remains a cost.

The forbidden score has already consumed probability mass during normalization. Masking the score before softmax makes the allowed weights sum to one; merely zeroing a value afterward generally does not.
There are 4×12+12×4=96 parameters. It transforms features within each position using shared weights; attention, rather than this independent FFN, mixes information across positions.

No. EOS is an input marker. Independent examples require an attention rule such as block-diagonal causal masking; an EOS marker alone does not zero cross-document attention weights.
Near-duplicates can cross the split and inflate performance. Group related or near-duplicate content before splitting and audit source lineage and evaluation-answer contamination.
Both estimate 1.2×10^20 training FLOPs. Equal estimated compute does not establish equal loss; data quality, optimization, and model size versus token allocation determine the outcome.
Weights require 4 GB, gradients 4 GB, and two FP32 Adam moment arrays 8 GB. Activations, buffers, and any additional state increase the total beyond this simplified estimate.

The tested training path can learn those examples, making some wiring failures less likely. It does not establish generalization. Inspect data mixture, contamination, overfitting, scoring consistency, and task slices.

It multiplies the loss before backward computation and divides gradients by the same scale before updating, which can prevent tiny low-precision gradients from rounding to zero. Clipping scaled gradients would apply a different effective threshold.
No. Two GB is the ideal per-worker share of that component only. Weights, gradients, activations, communication buffers, and temporary gathers can require additional memory.

Why initialize only one LoRA factor to zero rather than both?

Why can generating both task inputs and answers with the same teacher create apparently consistent but incorrect training data?
answers: Their target predictions are not directly scored, but the tokens remain available as context. Removing them from input is a different change that can destroy the conditional task.
A has 4×100 and B has 100×4 entries, totaling 800 rather than 10,000 unrestricted matrix entries. The frozen base still executes and requires storage.

One zero factor starts the added BA update at zero while a nonzero other factor enables a gradient into the zero factor. If both are zero, each factor’s gradient through the product is zero and learning stalls.

PPO clipping limits the surrogate incentive to move sampled-action probabilities relative to the policy that collected samples. Reference KL discourages distributional drift from a reference model. Neither is a universal hard update bound or a truth guarantee.
The margin is log 2−log 0.5=log 4. Sigmoid(log 4)=0.8. This relative objective need not increase the absolute probability of every preferred response.

A demonstration supplies desired token targets. An outcome reward evaluates a sampled continuation, and policy learning changes the probability of sampled actions using their estimated advantage. Both depend on the quality of their supervision.
It communicates the relative plausibility of the alternatives too. A compatible student distribution can learn those ratios, whereas one hard target discards that information.

The teacher can reproduce the same misconception in both. Validate with source evidence, calculations, execution, or independent review appropriate to the task; internal agreement is not independent verification.

questions: For probabilities [4/7,2/7,1/7], what does top-p sampling with p=0.8 retain?
Why can a schema-valid tool call still be unsafe or incorrect?
An 8000-token context reserves 500 for instructions, 1000 for history, and 1500 for output. How much remains for evidence?
How would you distinguish a retrieval failure from failure to use correctly retrieved evidence?
A remote write times out. Why is immediately retrying it potentially incorrect?
Should changing private policy documents primarily be learned through repeated fine-tuning?
Three independent attempts each succeed with probability 0.2. Is best-of-three deployed accuracy necessarily 0.488?
A search keeps only the highest-scoring partial path. Why can it miss the best complete path?
Why does adding a few-shot demonstration normally not change the stored parameter values?
Why can a strong reranker fail on a question containing an exact product identifier?
answers: The first two sorted tokens reach cumulative mass 6/7, which exceeds 0.8. After renormalization their probabilities are [2/3,1/3,0]. The result assumes probabilities were computed before this filtering step.

Schema validity checks structure and types, not resource authorization or semantic correctness. The executor must validate business rules, user permissions, and the actual referenced resource outside the model.
At most 5000 tokens before further role, separator, or tool-format overhead. Ensure the actual tokenizer and serving context-accounting convention match the estimate.

Keep question and model fixed and substitute verified evidence. Improvement points toward retrieval, chunk selection, or truncation. Continued failure points toward instructions, context use, or model capability.
The operation may have succeeded even though its response was lost. Check recorded status or use an idempotency key so a retry does not duplicate the effect.

First test authorized retrieval with freshness and source checks. It updates supplied evidence without retraining. Fine-tuning may help stable response behavior but is not a dependable mechanism for exact, rapidly changing factual access.

No. 1−0.8^3=0.488 is the probability at least one candidate succeeds under independence. A real selector must identify it; correlated mistakes, incomplete verifiers, and selection errors can lower delivered accuracy.

Conditional probabilities at later positions can reverse the ranking. An initially weaker branch can have a much stronger completion. A finite beam retains more candidates but still may prune the optimum.

It conditions the forward computation through input context. Ordinary inference has no gradient computation and optimizer update. Any model adaptation must be performed by a separate training procedure.

It can only reorder the candidate set it receives. If candidate retrieval omitted the exact supporting passage, reranking cannot recover it. Lexical or hybrid retrieval may improve coverage for identifiers.

questions: A score rises from 80 to 84 correct answers out of the same 100. Why inspect changed cases?
Why is high word overlap an inadequate factuality metric for summaries?
How would you detect position bias in a pairwise model judge?

Why is a system instruction saying “never leak data” insufficient protection for a retrieval tool?
What does deleting a private document from an index fail to guarantee?
How would you distinguish membership inference from extraction of a memorized training passage?
A model blocks every harmful test prompt by refusing every request. Which additional measurements reveal the failure?
answers: Four net wins can hide many regressions offset by gains. Paired inspection and important slices reveal what changed, while uncertainty estimates help judge whether the apparent gain is stable.
A short negation or changed number can reverse meaning while preserving most words. Check claim correctness and source support, using overlap only for the limited property it measures.

Randomize candidate order and repeat selected comparisons with the order swapped while hiding model identity. Inspect inconsistent judgments and validate against independent human labels under a fixed rubric.
Coverage is 80/100=0.8. Accuracy among answered requests is 72/80=0.9. Both are needed because avoiding difficult cases can inflate answered-case accuracy.
The model can be redirected or make mistakes. Enforce identity, document permissions, and outbound action checks independently of generated text; retrieved content cannot grant authorization.
It does not erase copies in caches or logs, nor remove any influence already learned in weights. Investigate each exposure route and validate the scope of any claimed deletion or unlearning.

Membership inference estimates whether an example was in training. Extraction attempts to reproduce content. They test different threats, and either must be evaluated separately from exposure through retrieval, tools, or logs.
Measure legitimate-task success and refusal appropriateness, including relevant languages and dialects. An attack-only metric hides over-refusal and uneven access to useful assistance.

Compute KV storage for 32 layers, one sequence, 4096 positions, eight KV heads, width 128, and two bytes per value.

For speculative sampling with q=[0.8,0.2] and p=[0.6,0.4], explain acceptance and rejection correction.
TTFT is 0.2 seconds and four following token intervals each take 0.05 seconds. What is five-token response time?
Why should weight-only and KV-cache quantization be evaluated separately for long concurrent requests?
answers: The model computes D’s states and key/value projections, appends its cache entries, attends to the allowed prefix, and produces logits for the next token. Earlier causal states can be reused if the prefix and configuration are unchanged.
2×32×1×4096×8×128×2=536870912 bytes, or 512 MiB. The factor two counts keys and values. Weights and runtime state are additional.

FlashAttention reduces attention memory traffic by tiled computation without materializing the full score matrix. Paged caches manage where sequence KV state is allocated to reduce waste and enable reuse. Neither by itself changes the causal attention semantics.

Independent processing counts 4400 prompt tokens; ideal reuse counts 2400, a saving of 2000. Runtime savings need not match that ratio because attention, cache lookup, and scheduling have their own costs.
A is accepted with probability 0.75 and B with probability one. Rejected A draws from normalized positive p−q, which selects B. Final mass is 0.6 on A and 0.4 on B, matching the target distribution.
Approximately 0.4 seconds: 0.2+(5−1)×0.05. Real queueing, variable interval times, and tools can change the result. Diagnose first-token and subsequent-token delays separately.

They compress different state. Weight compression can help the shared model footprint but leave sequence-dependent KV growth unchanged. Quantizing the KV cache targets that growth and has its own numerical and quality effects.

questions: X is an 8 × 4 batch and W is a 4 × 6 weight matrix. Compare splitting the batch across two workers with splitting W by output features. Which tensors are replicated, and how do the output shapes differ?

A scalar model predicts y = wx and uses loss (y − t)²/2. For x = 2, w = 1, and t = 3, compute the parameter gradient. If two pipeline stages split the graph at y, what derivative must cross the boundary?
Two replicas have equal parameters and receive identical averaged gradients, but one restored only model weights from a checkpoint. Why can the next Adam update differ?
Using vₜ = 0.9vₜ₋₁ + gₜ with v₀ = 0, gradients arrive as 2 and then −1. What are the momentum buffers? Why should a checkpoint specify the momentum convention?

A kernel performs 2 trillion operations and moves 20 billion device-memory bytes. Attainable compute is 100 trillion operations/second and bandwidth is 1 trillion bytes/second. Estimate its lower bound. What does doubling compute capacity buy?

A host timer around a GPU model call reports 0.2 milliseconds, but requests complete much later. How would you measure the operation correctly, and why might nonblocking transfers still fail to overlap compute?
On two nodes with four GPUs each, world rank 6 tries to select local GPU 6. What is wrong? Explain world rank, local rank, and subgroup rank.
Rank 0 calls All-Reduce and then All-Gather, while rank 1 calls All-Gather and then All-Reduce on the same process group. Both processes remain alive. Would adding a barrier fix the execution?
At 25 decimal gigabytes/second and 10 microseconds of startup per sequential message, compare one 1-megabyte message with 100 messages of 10 kilobytes. Ignore protocol overhead and contention.

Two GPU transfers each reach 25 gigabytes/second in isolation through the same 25-gigabyte/second network adapter. Why might concurrent execution deliver only about 25 gigabytes/second total? What does topology-aware placement change?
answers: The full result XW has shape 8 × 6. A batch split gives each worker X of shape 4 × 4 and a full 4 × 6 copy of W, producing distinct examples with outputs 4 × 6. An output-feature split gives each worker all of X and a 4 × 3 weight shard, producing 8 × 3 feature shards for the same examples. The first arrangement is data parallelism; the second partitions a layer. Whether feature shards must be gathered depends on the next operation. Worker count alone does not determine which dimension of useful work increased.

The prediction is 2, so the derivative with respect to y is y − t = −1. Multiplying by dy/dw = x = 2 gives dL/dw = −2. If the earlier stage owns the multiplication and the later stage computes the loss, the later stage sends dL/dy = −1 backward across the boundary. The earlier stage uses its local input to obtain the weight gradient. Sending only the scalar loss would not provide the upstream derivative needed to differentiate the earlier stage.

Adam also depends on its first-moment array, second-moment array, step count, hyperparameters, and learning-rate schedule. Different moments produce different normalized update directions, while different step counts change bias correction. Equal weights and gradients therefore do not establish equal next parameters. Restore optimizer and scheduler state as well as weights, and align which updates actually occurred. Restoring weights alone is sufficient for inference or an intentional optimization restart, but not for reproducing uninterrupted training.

The first buffer is 2; the second is 0.9 × 2 − 1 = 0.8. The second parameter update can still move in the earlier direction even though the latest gradient changed sign. Some implementations instead use a moving-average convention that multiplies the new gradient by 1 − momentum, or use other momentum variants. These states are not interchangeable without accounting for their definitions and update rules. A compatible checkpoint must preserve the optimizer configuration and buffers, not merely a tensor labeled momentum.

The arithmetic bound is 2/100 seconds = 20 milliseconds. The memory bound is 20/1000 seconds = 20 milliseconds. Under an ideal overlap model, elapsed time is at least their maximum, 20 milliseconds, rather than their sum. Doubling compute capacity reduces only the arithmetic bound to 10 milliseconds; the memory bound remains 20 milliseconds. Launch costs, dependencies, and inefficient accesses can make actual time larger. A useful optimization must reduce the limiting traffic or increase usable bandwidth before extra arithmetic capacity can improve this bound.

GPU submission is usually asynchronous, so the host timer may measure enqueueing rather than completed work. Warm up, then use device events or synchronize before and after an isolated measurement. Do not insert global synchronization into every production step, since that destroys overlap. A nonblocking transfer also needs ready source data, appropriate host memory and streams, free destination buffers, and an independent compute window. The copy and kernel may still compete for bandwidth or immediately wait on one another. Verify the timeline instead of inferring overlap from the API flag.

World rank identifies a worker in the eight-member world group; it is not a device ordinal on its node. Each host has only local GPU ordinals 0 through 3, so selecting local GPU 6 is invalid. Under a common contiguous mapping, world rank 6 belongs to the second node and local rank 2, but the launcher must define that mapping explicitly. A subgroup rank is its index among members of a particular smaller process group and can differ again. Log node, world rank, local rank, device, and group membership when diagnosing placement.

The first communication calls are incompatible, so the group may hang or report an error despite both processes being alive. A barrier does not make differently ordered collectives match; it can itself become another unmatched operation. Correct the shared communication schedule, including operation type, shapes, types, and group membership. Rank-dependent branches must not omit an operation required by peers. For asynchronous operations, also establish the documented completion dependency before consuming outputs or reusing input buffers. Being alive is not evidence that a worker can make useful progress.

Both choices carry 1,000,000 bytes, requiring 40 microseconds of payload time at the stated bandwidth. One message adds one startup, totaling approximately 50 microseconds. One hundred sequential messages add 1,000 microseconds of startups, totaling approximately 1,040 microseconds. Combining messages can amortize latency, but waiting to form a large message can delay its start and reduce communication–compute overlap. These are simplified sequential costs; pipelined or concurrent transport and shared-resource contention can change actual timings.

The transfers share the adapter, so their isolated bandwidths cannot be added as independent capacities. The same issue can occur at switches, device links, host staging buffers, or device memory. Topology-aware placement keeps high-frequency exchanges within well-connected groups when possible and reduces traffic through shared bottlenecks. Measure effective simultaneous bandwidth and contention, not just advertised link rates. When reporting volume, distinguish logical tensor bytes, per-rank sent bytes, receives, and aggregate traffic so that payload endpoints are not accidentally double-counted.

questions: Rank 0 holds [1, 2] and rank 1 holds [3, 4]. Give the results of sum All-Reduce, All-Gather, and sum Reduce-Scatter with equal one-element output shards. Which result is enough for sharded optimizer ownership?
An ideal ring All-Reduce uses four ranks and a 120-megabyte tensor on each rank. How many bytes does each rank send, how many rounds execute, and why does adding ranks eventually expose latency?

Two data-parallel workers report local mean gradients 2 and 6, based on 2 and 6 valid examples respectively. What is the correct global mean gradient? Why is averaging the two reported values incorrect?
A synchronized data-parallel run has the same global examples and initial weights as a single-device large-batch run, but their forward outputs differ. Must the collective implementation be wrong?
A distributed sampler pads its shards by repeating records so every worker executes the same number of evaluation steps. Why can accuracy be biased even if every All-Reduce is correct?
One evaluation worker has loss sum 20 over 10 examples; another has loss sum 90 over 30. How should mean loss be computed? Can the same average-of-worker-scores approach compute global ROC AUC?

Sixteen GPUs form two independent data replicas, each with four tensor workers and two pipeline stages. Each replica consumes four examples per microbatch and accumulates eight microbatches. What is the global batch, and what would an answer of 512 be counting?

A two-rank wrapper averages gradients. Over an entire accumulation window, rank 0 has loss sum S₀ over 3 valid tokens and rank 1 has S₁ over 7. How should each local loss sum be scaled to obtain the global mean token gradient?
You accumulate four equal-sized microbatches using DistributedDataParallel. Where should no_sync, gradient clearing, loss normalization, clipping, and optimizer.step occur?

A larger batch doubles examples/second but needs twice as many processed examples to reach the same held-out quality. What happened to time to quality? Does linearly scaling the learning rate guarantee a fix?
A recommendation model has an enormous embedding table, but each batch touches only a small set of IDs. Why might sharded parameter ownership help, and what can still become a bottleneck?

For loss θ²/2, an asynchronous worker reads θ = 2, but the owner reaches θ = −1 before applying its gradient. With learning rate 0.1, compare the stale and fresh updates. Why are multiple local SGD steps also different from synchronous gradient averaging?
answers: Sum All-Reduce gives [4, 6] to both ranks. All-Gather concatenates the distinct inputs and gives [1, 2, 3, 4] to both ranks; it performs no addition. Sum Reduce-Scatter gives [4] to rank 0 and [6] to rank 1 under the stated shard order. If each optimizer owner updates only its assigned parameter shard, its reduced gradient shard can be sufficient. Reconstructing the full reduced gradient everywhere would add communication and redundant storage. Updated parameter availability for subsequent computation is a separate requirement.

Reduce-Scatter and All-Gather each take p − 1 = 3 rounds, with M/p = 30 megabytes sent per rank per round. Across both phases, each rank sends 2(p − 1)M/p = 180 megabytes over six rounds. This is sent volume per rank, excluding receives and protocol overhead. As rank count grows, the volume approaches 2M, but the number of startup rounds keeps increasing. Small tensors or strongly scaled workloads can therefore become latency-dominated even though per-rank payload volume stays bounded.

There are 8 valid examples. Their aggregate gradient sum is 2 × 2 + 6 × 6 = 40, so the correct global mean is 5. Averaging local means gives 4 and assigns each worker equal weight rather than each example equal weight. Aggregate weighted sums and valid counts. If a wrapper already averages across p workers, scale each local loss sum by p divided by the total valid count before backward. For masked-token objectives, the relevant count is valid target tokens rather than batch rows.

No. Equivalence requires the same function and objective, not merely the same examples and weights. Batch normalization can use different local batch statistics, so each worker may evaluate a different function from one global batch. Synchronized statistics can address that specific discrepancy but add communication. Dropout masks, augmentation, precision, and kernel or reduction order can also differ. First compare forward outputs with stochastic behavior controlled and a model without unintended batch dependencies. Then compare loss denominators, gradients, and optimizer transitions to localize the first mismatch.

The repeated records enter the numerator and denominator more than once, changing the evaluation population. A correct reduction cannot undo incorrect record ownership. Use duplicate-free evaluation shards with safe collective participation, or track record identifiers and exclude repeated padding before aggregation. Distinguish sampler-level repetition from token padding and loader-level dropping; their combined behavior matters. Equal-length shards are convenient for training execution but are not sufficient evidence of a valid evaluation sample.

Aggregate the loss sums and counts: (20 + 90)/(10 + 30) = 2.75. Averaging the local means, 2 and 3, gives 2.5 and incorrectly gives equal weight to unequal-sized groups. Global receiver operating characteristic area under the curve, or ROC AUC, generally depends on cross-worker ordering of positive and negative prediction scores. Even count-weighted averaging of local AUC values misses those cross-worker pairs. Gather the required score/label information or use a deliberately specified distributed approximation; do not treat every metric as an additive scalar.

The global batch is 2 data replicas × 4 examples × 8 accumulated microbatches = 64 examples per optimizer update. The tensor and pipeline workers cooperate on those same examples, so multiplying by all 16 physical GPUs would count model collaborators as additional data replicas and produce the incorrect 512. Specify the logical data-parallel group and accumulation boundary before using a batch-size formula. Pipeline microbatches should not be multiplied again if they are already the microbatches counted in the accumulation window.

The complete update has N = 10 valid tokens and p = 2 rank contributions. Differentiate each local loss sum multiplied by p/N = 0.2. The wrapper then averages those two gradients, giving (∇S₀ + ∇S₁)/10. Do not independently average each rank by its local token count, and do not divide by the accumulation count again after already normalizing the complete token sum. The count must cover the same update window as the accumulated gradients; masks and partial final microbatches must be included correctly.

Clear gradients before the accumulation window. For the first three microbatches, place both forward and backward inside no_sync so redundant reductions are avoided.
