Use the normal synchronized forward/backward for the final microbatch, which synchronizes the accumulated gradients. Divide each mean loss by four under the equal-size assumption. Unscale mixed-precision gradients if needed, clip once after the complete gradient is ready, and call optimizer.step once. Advance the update-based scheduler once as appropriate. Unequal valid counts require whole-window weighted normalization instead of blindly dividing every local mean by four.

Under these exact rates, time to quality is unchanged: twice the required examples divided by twice the throughput gives the same duration. If the faster run uses more devices, its total accelerator-hours can be worse. Linear learning-rate scaling is a heuristic that can work in some regimes, often with warmup, but is not a guarantee for arbitrary optimizers, batches, or objectives. Compare complete learning curves, update counts, and cost under a defined quality target. Also check gradient normalization before attributing a changed effective step size to optimization behavior.

Assign embedding rows and their optimizer state to owners, route row lookups to them, and return only gradients for accessed rows. This avoids fetching and exchanging the complete table for every batch. Repeated IDs can be combined before sending contributions. Popular IDs can create hot shards, and network exchange or owner-side optimizer work can dominate even when access is sparse. Define read versions and update consistency explicitly. Sparse row access is different from fully sharded dense training that reconstructs complete layer weights before executing dense operations.

The stale gradient is 2, so applying it to the current value gives −1 − 0.1 × 2 = −1.2. The fresh gradient would be −1, producing −0.9 instead. The stale update moves opposite to the current descent direction. Several local SGD steps similarly evaluate later gradients at replica-specific parameters, so averaging final weights generally differs from aggregating gradients at a shared model before every update. One local step with ordinary SGD and equal weights can match synchronous averaging; adaptive optimizer states introduce additional reconciliation requirements.

questions: A one-billion-parameter model uses 2-byte weights, 2-byte gradients, a 4-byte master weight, and two 4-byte Adam moment arrays. Compute persistent state memory. Why can it still fail on a device with more free memory than this total?
An FP16 distributed run gets nonfinite gradients. What does loss scaling do, and what must be synchronized before clipping and updating? Would BF16 eliminate all numerical issues?

Using the 16-byte ledger from the memory lesson and eight workers, compare ideal persistent bytes per parameter for replication, optimizer-only sharding, optimizer-plus-gradient sharding, and full state sharding.

Assume equal parameter and gradient byte widths. A fully sharded step gathers parameters once before forward, frees them, gathers again before backward, and Reduce-Scatters gradients. Compare ideal ring-style sent bytes with replicated gradient All-Reduce, and explain why grouping layers matters.

For X = [1, 2] and W = [3, 4]ᵀ, row partitioning computes local outputs 3 and 8. Should they be concatenated or summed? What backward communication is required for a column-partitioned matrix multiplication with replicated input gradients?

How does sequence activation sharding differ from context parallelism? For two remote single-key attention blocks with scores 0 and log(2), and values 1 and 4, why is averaging their locally normalized outputs incorrect?

In an ideal balanced fill–drain pipeline with four stages and eight microbatches, estimate utilization. Would increasing to sixteen microbatches necessarily improve the measured step time at fixed global batch size?

A pipeline developer updates a stage’s weights as soon as each microbatch finishes backward. Why can this violate synchronous training? How does one-forward–one-backward scheduling reduce memory without requiring this change?

How do activation checkpointing and offloading save device memory differently? If 4 decimal gigabytes must leave a GPU and return over a 25-gigabyte/second effective link with no overlap, what is the transfer lower bound?

An engineer says FlashAttention makes dense attention linear in sequence length because it avoids storing the full score matrix. What is the distinction between memory traffic and arithmetic complexity?

A mixture-of-experts layer routes 12 tokens to one of four experts. Its capacity factor is 1.25, with capacity ceil(cNk/E). Loads are [6, 2, 2, 2]. What is capacity, and what are the consequences of overflow policies?

Why can a sparsely activated expert model run slower than a dense model with similar active arithmetic? Trace forward and backward communication rather than reasoning only from active parameter count.
answers: The specified ledger uses 2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 bytes per parameter, or 16 decimal gigabytes for one billion parameters. Peak memory also includes saved activations, temporary kernel workspaces, communication buffers, casts, gathered parameter groups, and allocator/runtime overhead. These lifetimes can overlap. A different implementation might retain FP32 gradients or use its canonical FP32 parameters instead of an independent master copy, so the 16-byte figure is conditional on the stated design. Measure the entire representative step, including gathers and optimizer execution.

Loss scaling multiplies the loss before backward to keep small FP16 gradients representable; it does not repair invalid arithmetic or make an overflowing gradient safe. Maintain a consistent scale across an accumulation window, unscale before clipping and updating, detect nonfinite values, and coordinate any skipped-update decision across cooperating workers. Keep optimizer and scheduler transitions consistent too. BF16 has a much wider exponent range than FP16 and often needs no loss scaling, but has limited significand precision. Reduction order, low-precision communication, unstable operations, and unsuitable learning rates can still cause error or divergence.

With weight bytes 2, gradient bytes 2, and optimizer-related bytes 12 including the master weight, replication uses 16 bytes per parameter per rank. Sharding only optimizer-related state gives 2 + 2 + 12/8 = 5.5. Also sharding gradients gives 2 + (2 + 12)/8 = 3.75. Sharding all persistent states gives 16/8 = 2. These are ideal ownership budgets, not full peak-memory predictions. Temporarily generated gradients, gathered weights, activations, padding/alignment, and communication buffers remain relevant. State exactly what is included in optimizer state to avoid counting the master weight twice.

If the complete parameter or gradient tensor has M bytes across p workers, each gather or Reduce-Scatter sends approximately (p − 1)M/p per rank. The described sharded step therefore sends 3(p − 1)M/p, versus 2(p − 1)M/p for replicated gradient All-Reduce. Sharding buys persistent memory, not an unconditional traffic reduction. Small layer groups reduce temporarily gathered memory and can overlap the next gather with compute; overly small groups pay more startup overhead. Retaining full weights avoids a repeated gather but increases memory. Precision, accumulation policy, and the actual group topology can change the comparison.

The row-partitioned outputs are partial sums over the input-feature dimension, so add them to obtain the scalar 11. Concatenating [3, 8] would change the operation. Column partitioning instead produces distinct output-feature shards Yᵢ = XWᵢ. Its backward computes local input-gradient contributions GᵢWᵢᵀ that must be summed to reconstruct the replicated input gradient. Weight gradients for the column shards remain locally shaped as XᵀGᵢ, subject to any separate data-replica aggregation. Tensor layout determines whether values are distinct partitions or contributions to the same result.

Sequence activation sharding can divide token positions for operations such as per-token layer normalization, then convert layouts around neighboring operations. Context parallelism divides attention positions, whose queries may need remote keys and values. Its partial attention outputs must preserve global softmax normalization. The two keys have relative unnormalized weights 1 and 2, so the correct result is (1 × 1 + 2 × 4)/3 = 3. Locally normalizing each single-key block yields 1 and 4; averaging gives 2.5 and loses their relative probability mass. Combine block maxima, denominator sums, and weighted numerators on a common numerical scale.

The ideal utilization is m/(m + s − 1) = 8/11, about 72.7%; the bubble fraction is 3/11. Sixteen microbatches would improve the ideal fraction to 16/19, about 84.2%. However, fixed global batch size means smaller microbatches, which may make matrix kernels less efficient and increase launch or communication overhead. The estimate assumes balanced stages, equal forward/backward timing, and negligible boundary transfers. Compare end-to-end step time and activation memory, not just the analytical bubble fraction.

Microbatches intended to contribute to one synchronous update should use the same logical parameter version. Updating after each microbatch can make later forwards or backwards refer to inconsistent versions, changing the algorithm and potentially invalidating saved activations. Accumulate correctly weighted gradients and update at a shared boundary. One-forward–one-backward scheduling alternates ready forward and backward work after warmup, allowing earlier activations to be retired sooner than in fill–drain. Scheduling backward earlier does not require updating parameters early. Shared/tied parameters and additional data replicas also need their contributions combined consistently.

Activation checkpointing retains selected graph boundaries and reruns internal forward computation during backward, trading arithmetic for saved intermediates. Offloading stores values in host memory or another tier and later transfers them back, trading device capacity for staging memory and transfer time. The round trip moves 8 gigabytes, giving 8/25 seconds = 0.32 seconds before other overhead. Recomputation must preserve random masks and relevant state so it differentiates the same function. Offloading needs a valid prefetch/lifetime schedule and cannot hide transfers without independent work and sufficient bandwidth. Neither is a durable recovery checkpoint.

A tiled, input/output-aware implementation can avoid materializing the full sequence-by-sequence score matrix in device memory by maintaining running softmax and output statistics. This reduces large intermediates and memory transfers and can make exact attention much faster. It does not remove the dense query–key token-pair computations, whose arithmetic still grows quadratically with sequence length under ordinary dense attention assumptions. Distinguish allocation size, traffic between memory levels, and mathematical operation count. Approximate, sparse, or windowed attention changes which pairs are computed and is a different mechanism.

With N = 12, k = 1, E = 4, and c = 1.25, per-expert capacity is ceil(3.75) = 4. The first expert has two assignments beyond capacity despite spare capacity on other experts. Dropping excess routed contributions changes the computation and can affect quality; rerouting changes expert selection; retaining all assignments requires variable work and potentially more memory. Padding every expert to a fixed capacity simplifies shapes but wastes slots. Increasing total experts or aggregate capacity alone does not guarantee balanced routing or equal execution times.

Forward routes and packs tokens, exchanges them with expert owners, executes the selected experts, returns results, and restores token order for weighted combination. Backward must deliver gradients through the same assignments and combine repeated token contributions correctly. All-to-All traffic, routing metadata, small per-expert batches, memory pressure, and a hot expert can dominate saved arithmetic. Inactive experts still need parameter storage somewhere. If expert weights are replicated or tensor-sharded, their gradient synchronization groups must match that ownership. Profile the complete dispatch/compute/return path and slowest owner, not just expert matrix FLOPs.

questions: A device mesh has two data replicas, four tensor workers per stage, and two pipeline stages. How many devices are used? Which coordinates define tensor and data groups, and is state sharding necessarily another multiplicative axis?

A model needs tensor and pipeline parallelism across two eight-GPU nodes. Why might keeping tensor groups within a node and connecting pipeline stages across nodes help? When could that placement still be poor?
For fixed work taking one second on one worker and 0.2 seconds on eight, compute speedup and efficiency. Separately, what does Amdahl’s law predict with a 5% serial fraction on eight workers?

One run reaches a held-out quality target in 10 hours on eight accelerators; another reaches it in six hours on 32. Which is faster and which consumes fewer accelerator-hours? How does this differ from weak-scaling throughput?

A trace shows 20 milliseconds of compute, 12 milliseconds of communication, and 8 milliseconds where they overlap. What is elapsed time under a two-category model? Why can separately measured kernel times make this prediction inaccurate?
You halve gradient bucket size and prefetch two additional sharded layers, but step time gets worse and peak memory rises. Give a plausible explanation and the trace evidence you would collect.

Four synchronous workers finish their compute in [10, 10, 10, 30] milliseconds before a shared synchronization. What is compute utilization over that interval? Why might equal sequence counts still produce this pattern?

Packing several short text sequences into one tensor improves utilization. What correctness checks are needed? If a faster data worker then handles more valid tokens per update, how must aggregation change?
answers: The simple rectangular mesh uses 2 × 4 × 2 = 16 devices. A tensor group fixes the replica and pipeline-stage coordinates while varying tensor position. A data group fixes stage and tensor position while varying independent data replicas. Pipeline neighbors connect corresponding stage boundaries. State sharding can operate within that existing data group, so multiplying by an additional shard degree would double-count devices in that arrangement. Additional context or expert layouts need explicit ownership and group definitions rather than a product of every technique name.

Tensor groups can exchange partial results repeatedly within every layer, whereas pipeline communication occurs at stage boundaries. Keeping frequent tensor exchange on strong local links can avoid repeated inter-node latency and bandwidth costs. But stage-boundary activations may be large, stage times may be unbalanced, and data-gradient, state-gather, context, or expert traffic can still contend for shared adapters. A different placement can be better when those costs dominate. Estimate actual byte sizes, frequency, group membership, peak memory, and concurrent paths, then validate with a representative trace.

The measured speedup is 1/0.2 = 5 and parallel efficiency is 5/8 = 62.5%. With serial fraction f = 0.05 and ideal division of the remaining work, Amdahl’s bound is 1/(0.05 + 0.95/8), approximately 5.93, or 74.1% efficiency. Communication and imbalance can make real scaling worse than that ideal model. The comparison must hold useful work fixed. If the model cannot execute on one worker, use a stated feasible multi-worker baseline and normalize by the resource ratio instead of inventing a single-worker runtime.

The 32-device run reaches the target sooner: six versus ten hours. The eight-device run consumes fewer accelerator-hours: 80 versus 192. Device-hours are only a proxy if device types or prices differ; then compare stated cost or normalized capacity. Weak scaling grows work with resources, such as holding local batch size fixed while global batch increases, so examples/second can improve without the same change in time to target quality. Report the quality criterion, global batch, optimizer settings, end-to-end duration, and failure/checkpoint overhead relevant to the decision.

Elapsed time is 20 + 12 − 8 = 24 milliseconds. Perfect overlap could reduce it to max(20, 12) = 20 milliseconds in that simplified model. Compute and communication may compete for device-memory bandwidth, execution resources, or the same interconnect, so their co-running durations can differ from their isolated durations. Host work, input stalls, and dependencies add other categories. Optimize the measured critical path and final exposed communication tail rather than treating the sum of isolated operation times as a faithful trace.

Smaller buckets may become ready sooner but increase startup count and reduce transfer efficiency. Extra prefetch may keep several full parameter groups live, increasing peak memory and causing allocation pressure. Concurrent collectives can serialize on a communicator or compete for the same network and memory bandwidth rather than hiding one another. Inspect gradient readiness, collective start/end times, the last required reduction, stalls before layers, allocation peaks, and compute slowdown during concurrent transfers. Compare one controlled change at a time with the same workload, precision, and update semantics.

The interval lasts 30 milliseconds and offers 4 × 30 = 120 worker-milliseconds of capacity. Useful compute occupies 10 + 10 + 10 + 30 = 60, so utilization is 50% under this simplified model. Equal sequence counts can hide different lengths, padding waste, attention pair counts, or routed expert loads. Separate persistent partition imbalance from transient loader, network, or hardware delays. Balance measured work and shared-resource pressure, while retaining correctly weighted gradient contributions and compatible collective participation.

Independent packed sequences must not accidentally attend across their boundaries. Validate causal/block masks, positions as required by the model, target alignment, padding masks, and valid-token counts. Bucketing and packing also change ordering or mixing, so preserve the intended sampling distribution. If a faster worker processes more valid tokens, a token-weighted objective must give its loss sum proportionally more contribution through the common global denominator. Equally averaging local means would underweight that worker’s tokens. Do not drop slow workers or variable-sized records without an explicit objective and synchronization policy.

questions: A distributed training loss is finite and decreases, but validation is worse than a single-device reference. How would you localize a correctness error without assuming the decreasing loss proves the implementation?
Two owners hold unique gradient shards [3] and [4]. Clip the global norm to 1. What goes wrong if each clips locally, or if replicated copies are included twice in the norm?
One rank detects a nonfinite gradient and skips Adam while a peer updates. Later you set the same seed on both ranks, but results still diverge. What state and reproducibility issues remain?
Rendezvous succeeds on all nodes, but the first large collective fails. Does successful membership discovery prove the network path is healthy? What evidence should you inspect?
At step 500, one worker exhausts its input shard and exits backward while the others hang. Why is a longer timeout or an extra barrier insufficient? How would you recover?

A checkpoint writer asynchronously reads live tensors while training advances. It publishes a manifest after only some shard uploads finish. Why are both decisions unsafe, and what should a resumable snapshot include?

Checkpoint overhead is 10 seconds and the mean time between job failures is 3,600 seconds. Under the guide’s simple independent-failure model, estimate the interval minimizing C/I + λI/2. What assumptions could invalidate the estimate?
A job restarts from eight to four data replicas using a sharded checkpoint. What must change besides loading the weight files, and why might the continuation no longer be bitwise identical?
answers: Use a small case with the same examples, initial parameters, objective weighting, optimizer state, precision, and update boundary. Compare forward outputs, loss sums and counts, individual logical gradients, and the next persistent state in order. Control randomness and batch-dependent behavior. Use unequal local counts and asymmetric examples to expose normalization bugs; identical data on all workers can hide them. Reconstruct small partitioned tensors only for diagnosis and check tiny gradients with finite differences. Identify the first mismatching boundary before attributing the problem to optimization or distributed performance.

The unique global norm is sqrt(3² + 4²) = 5. Apply a shared scale of 1/5, giving [0.6] and [0.8], whose global norm is 1. Independent shard clipping gives [1] and [1], with norm sqrt(2), violating the global threshold. Counting duplicated full gradients also inflates the norm and over-clips. Sum squared values across unique ownership groups, with replication handled explicitly, then share the resulting scale. In mixed precision, unscale first and coordinate any nonfinite/skip decision before updating parameters.

The ranks may now have different weights, Adam moments, step counts, scaler values, and scheduler positions; reseeding does not reconcile those states. Cooperating workers need a consistent skip decision and restored shared update boundary. Seeds also do not guarantee the same random draws were consumed in the same order. Data replicas and tensor partitions can need different or coordinated random streams depending on the operation. Floating-point reduction order, nondeterministic kernels, device type, and worker-count changes can prevent bitwise identity even for correct equivalent objectives. Compare with justified absolute and relative tolerances.

Rendezvous establishes coordination and membership, not the health or suitability of every later transport path. Verify rank-to-device mapping, selected interfaces, backend compatibility, group membership, types, shapes, and accessible communication paths. Large transfers can additionally expose memory pressure, transport limits, or contention absent in small startup exchanges. Preserve the earliest rank-specific exception; later timeouts may be consequences. Test representative transfers on the same topology, then a small faithful model step, before adding the full input and memory workload.

The required communication participant is missing. A longer timeout merely delays detection, and a barrier cannot supply the absent gradient or repair incompatible control flow. Choose an explicit uneven-input policy that preserves the intended weighting and keeps all required collectives compatible, or terminate the step coherently. A framework-specific join mechanism must also account for any additional non-wrapper collectives. After a failed communication group, follow the backend’s recovery contract; commonly restart the coordinated worker group from a fully committed checkpoint instead of allowing surviving ranks to make unmatched updates.

Reading tensors that updates can mutate risks mixing logical steps; asynchronous storage needs a stable, isolated snapshot with correct device dependencies and staging memory. Publishing before all required shards are durable can advertise an incomplete checkpoint. Save under a fresh generation, finish and verify all required writes, then publish a commit record using the storage system’s actual guarantees. Include parameters, buffers, optimizer moments and step, scheduler/scaler, host/device randomness, consumed data and sampler state, and layout/configuration. Prefer an optimizer-update boundary unless partially accumulated gradients and pipeline work are captured explicitly.

With C = 10 and λ = 1/3600 per second, the minimizing interval is sqrt(2C/λ) = sqrt(72,000), approximately 268 seconds of useful training. More frequent saves waste writing time; less frequent saves lose more work per failure. The model assumes infrequent independent failures, small checkpoint overhead, and roughly uniform lost progress averaging half an interval. Correlated failures, variable steps, asynchronous staging/storage contention, checkpoint failures, and significant restart time can change the optimum. Use the job-level failure rate, not blindly one device’s failure rate.

Reconstruct logical parameters, optimizer state, buffers, and metadata into a supported four-replica layout; rebuild process groups and unique data ownership. With unchanged local batch and accumulation, global batch halves, so adjust them if the same effective batch is intended. Restore consumed records rather than merely the loader’s furthest prefetched offset, and apply an explicit replay policy. Scheduler/scaler and optimizer-step semantics must remain aligned. Different sharding, reduction order, kernel shapes, random streams, or example order can prevent bitwise identity despite a correct restored logical state. Verify the quality and objective contract rather than promising exact replay across arbitrary layouts.

questions: A stable service completes 80 requests/second with 0.1 seconds mean arrival-to-completion time. What does Little’s law imply about average concurrency? Why is that not a safe concurrency cap or tail-latency guarantee?

A service doubles saturated GPU throughput by waiting for larger batches, but users complain about slower responses. Which latency components and capacity metrics would you compare before adding replicas?

For 32 attention layers, eight key/value heads, head width 128, two bytes per cache element, and 4,096 retained tokens, compute raw KV-cache bytes for one request and for eight requests. Which overheads are excluded?
Why can prompt prefill and small-batch decode have different bottlenecks? A model has many query heads but fewer key/value heads; which count determines cache size?
Eight GPUs can run four two-GPU replicas or one eight-GPU replica. What evidence would make either choice preferable, and why should a training parallelization plan not simply be reused?
A front-end process of a model-parallel replica is healthy, but one attention shard fails. Can the router keep sending requests to the front-end? Where does an active request’s KV cache live?
A paged cache uses 16-token blocks and a request retains 17 tokens. How many slots are allocated? Why do continuous batching and chunked prefill need more than a maximum active-request count?
Two requests share the same visible text prefix, and weights are quantized from 16 to four bits. Can their cache always be shared, and should total memory or latency improve fourfold?

Moving prefill and decode to separate nodes requires transferring a 512-mebibyte KV cache at 25 decimal gigabytes/second. Estimate payload-transfer latency. What would justify paying it, and what if the pools use different tensor degrees?

A decode pool is overloaded and autoscaling starts a new model-parallel replica. Meanwhile an old replica is being removed during a rolling model update. How should admission, stateful requests, cache reuse, and streaming retries be handled?
answers: Little’s law gives mean in-flight requests L = λW = 80 × 0.1 = 8 under consistent system boundaries. It is an average, not a maximum or a statement that all requests last 0.1 seconds. Bursts, variable request lengths, and long service times can require greater instantaneous concurrency and build queues. If measuring only the waiting queue, use waiting time rather than total response time. Size admission, memory, capacity headroom, and deadlines from the workload distribution and response objectives, not from this average alone.

Separate routing, queueing, batch-formation delay, model execution, and output delivery. Larger batches can improve arithmetic and weight reuse while adding waiting and memory pressure, especially at low traffic. Compare end-to-end and high-percentile latency under representative bursts and request lengths, plus accepted goodput meeting the response objective. Use a maximum batching wait as well as a batch-size limit. Independent replicas can add capacity, but poor routing, head-of-line blocking, unbounded queues, or immediate retries can still violate objectives. Preserve headroom for replica failure and startup delays.

Keys and values require 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 × 4096 = 536,870,912 bytes, or 512 mebibytes, for one request. Eight such requests require 4 gibibytes. This is raw cache payload, excluding page allocation waste, block tables, padding, alignment, runtime buffers, weights, live activations, and communication. Actual per-device use follows the cache ownership: some heads or other values may be replicated rather than evenly sharded. State whether all layers retain this full context; windows or different layer structures change the calculation.

Prefill processes known prompt positions in parallel and often exposes large matrix operations with high arithmetic intensity. Ordinary decode advances each sequence one token at a time, repeatedly reading weights and growing cached state for relatively little new arithmetic, so small-batch decode is often memory-bandwidth limited. Batching, context length, kernels, quantization, and network exchange can change the limiting resource. Use key/value head count in the KV-memory equation, not query-head count. Grouped-query or multi-query attention shares keys/values architecturally; it is not a generally safe runtime conversion for an arbitrary trained model.

Compare model and active-cache fit, per-request latency, aggregate goodput, queueing, batch sizes, and exposed forward communication. A wider replica can provide necessary memory or faster useful arithmetic, but small decode shards may pay collective startup repeatedly and offer fewer independent scheduling units. More replicas can serve independent traffic and isolate failures when the complete model and request state fit. Inference removes optimizer/gradient state and backward communication while adding variable persistent request state. Recompute its memory and critical-path budget instead of assuming the training placement remains optimal.

The front-end alone cannot execute the complete model; route only when every required partition of the replica is ready. A missing tensor or pipeline shard can stall or invalidate all requests using that replica. Cache ownership follows the attention layout: pipeline stages retain their layers’ cache, and tensor/context workers may partition or replicate heads or positions. Do not assume cache divides evenly by total GPU count. Recovery must rebuild a compatible complete replica and restore, migrate, or recompute each request’s state, rather than treating surviving devices as automatically usable independent replicas.

The request needs ceil(17/16) = 2 blocks, or 32 token slots, with 15 unused slots in its final block. Paging reduces contiguous over-reservation and some fragmentation, but does not eliminate live cache bytes or metadata. Continuous batching changes membership at token-iteration boundaries while preserving separate histories and masks. Admission must track token work, growing cache demand, prefill budgets, and latency priorities. Chunked prefill can limit interference with active decode, but smaller chunks add overhead and must attend to the proper preceding context. Equal request counts can represent very different work and memory.

Cache reuse requires matching token IDs, model version, positions, masks, adapters, and other relevant execution settings; visible text alone is insufficient. Shared blocks should remain immutable, with copy-on-write when a request must modify a shared partially filled block. Four-bit weights ideally reduce raw weight payload by four relative to 16 bits, but scales, packing, alignment, unquantized values, activations, KV caches, and runtime buffers remain. Latency also depends on dequantization, kernel support, communication, and the actual bottleneck. Cache quantization is a separate policy whose output quality and long-context behavior need evaluation.

The payload is 536,870,912 bytes; divided by 25 billion bytes/second it takes approximately 21.5 milliseconds before setup, contention, packing, or queueing. Disaggregation can be worthwhile if less prefill/decode interference and better independent resource allocation improve response-constrained goodput enough to outweigh handoff cost. Compare with colocated and chunked-prefill designs on representative traffic. Different tensor or pipeline degrees may require cache redistribution and layout conversion rather than a direct one-to-one copy. Include that work, the handoff boundary, metadata, and any first-token responsibility in the latency and correctness budget.

Do not route to the new replica until weights, devices, communication, and every required shard are ready. Account for startup time when controlling queues and backpressure. Drain the old replica or explicitly migrate/recompute compatible request state before removing it. Version weights, tokenizer, adapters, generation settings, cache format, and layout; incompatible caches cannot be reused merely because shapes match. A retry may recompute state from the prompt plus accepted output, but streaming needs request IDs and offsets to avoid duplicated output. Exact sampled continuation requires the necessary preserved request state and a supported replay contract. Autoscaling capacity alone does not supply those semantics.

questions: A product team wants to choose a banner using click feedback. When would supervised learning, a contextual bandit, or full reinforcement learning be justified?
Two policies have the same estimated mean return. One was tested on five episodes and another on 5,000. What additional evidence is needed before claiming they are equally good?
A value predictor is v = wx with loss (v − y)²/2. At x = 2, w = 1, y = 3, what gradient does backpropagation compute, and what does SGD with learning rate 0.1 do?
A robot policy observes its current position but not velocity. The same position sometimes requires braking and sometimes acceleration. Is adding a larger network sufficient?
An episode receives rewards 2, 0, and 10. With discount 0.9, compute its initial return. What changes if the discount becomes zero?
A rollout stops at an external collection time limit after reward 1, with successor value 5 and discount 0.9. Compare the target with a genuine terminal transition.
Explain Vπ(s), Qπ(s,a), and advantage without treating immediate reward and long-term value as interchangeable. Can a negative immediate reward have positive advantage?
For one action, the next outcome is reward 2 and successor value 4 with probability 0.75, or terminal reward −2 with probability 0.25. Compute its Bellman value at discount 0.9.
A system has high prediction accuracy for immediate rewards but makes poor decisions over long sessions. What mismatch would you investigate before choosing a more complex RL algorithm?

A stochastic policy assigns action probabilities while the environment has uncertain transitions. Why are these different sources of randomness, and why record both policy and environment settings during evaluation?
answers: Use supervised prediction when the task is to estimate an outcome from representative labeled examples and the decision policy does not need to learn through interaction. A contextual bandit models action-dependent feedback for the current decision, including exploration and logged propensities. Full reinforcement learning is justified when actions materially change future states or opportunities, so delayed consequences determine value. Do not introduce long-horizon RL merely because rewards are observed: establish the sequential effect, feedback access, and a simple baseline first.

Separate variability of episode outcomes from uncertainty in the estimated mean. Examine episode counts, variance, uncertainty intervals, seeds, initial states, and the evaluation distribution. Five episodes may provide little evidence, particularly for rare failures or heavy-tailed returns. The 5,000 episodes also need to be representative and sufficiently independent; repeated nearly identical states do not establish broad generalization. Evaluate important failure probabilities and distribution slices rather than selecting a policy from equal point estimates alone.

The prediction is 2 and the derivative with respect to the prediction is 2 − 3 = −1. Applying the chain rule gives dL/dw = −1 × 2 = −2. Stochastic gradient descent changes the weight to 1 − 0.1 × (−2) = 1.2, producing prediction 2.4. Backpropagation calculates sensitivities; the optimizer performs the update. In RL the target may itself be a learned estimate, so specify whether it is detached before treating this as an ordinary fixed-target regression gradient.

The observation may omit information required for predicting the next outcome. Position alone is generally not Markov when dynamics depend on velocity. A larger feed-forward network cannot reliably distinguish identical inputs that require different actions. Add relevant measurements, a short history, a recurrent state, or another state estimator, then test whether decisions improve under the actual observation process. The environment can have a Markov state even when the agent receives a partially informative observation.

The initial discounted return is 2 + 0.9 × 0 + 0.9² × 10 = 10.1. The first reward is not discounted. With discount zero, return is just 2, so later consequences no longer affect this initial objective. Discounting changes which behavior is preferred; it is not only an optimization stabilizer. In a continuing task with constant reward r and discount below one, the value scale is r/(1 − discount), so changing the discount also changes typical target magnitudes.

For an external cutoff in a continuing task, bootstrap from the final actual successor: the target is 1 + 0.9 × 5 = 5.5. For genuine task termination, no continuation remains, so the target is 1. Do not bootstrap from the automatic reset observation, and do not continue trace recursion into an unrelated episode. A true finite task deadline is different from a collection limit and may legitimately have zero continuation, with remaining time included in the task state when needed.

Vπ is expected future return from a state when following policy π; Qπ conditions additionally on taking a particular first action. Advantage is Qπ(s,a) − Vπ(s), comparing that action with the policy average in the same state. A costly action can have positive advantage if it leads to sufficiently better future outcomes. The reward is the immediate feedback, while value aggregates its discounted consequences. These quantities depend on the policy and objective, so changing either can change their rankings.

The expected one-step reward-plus-continuation is 0.75 × (2 + 0.9 × 4) + 0.25 × (−2) = 3.7. The terminal branch has no continuation term. This is a policy-evaluation backup if the successor value evaluates the specified policy. Replacing that successor with an optimal value or maximizing over future actions changes the interpretation. Average across possible environment outcomes; do not choose the best stochastic outcome as though the agent controlled it.

Check whether the modeled target captures action-dependent future consequences, the actual session horizon, and the business or task objective. Predicting immediate reward accurately is not the same as estimating return or choosing a good policy. Also inspect action coverage, delayed feedback attribution, observation quality, and whether the evaluation policy changes the data distribution. Establish a contextual-bandit or simple control baseline where appropriate. Complexity cannot repair a reward that omits the important outcome or a state that hides necessary information.

Policy randomness determines which action is selected from a state; environment randomness determines which outcome follows a chosen action. A deterministic policy can still have variable returns in a stochastic environment. Conversely, a stochastic policy can vary even in deterministic dynamics. Evaluation should state whether actions are sampled or selected deterministically, and should control or vary environment seeds and initial states deliberately. Otherwise an apparent policy improvement may reflect different test conditions rather than better expected behavior.

questions: If an environment model is known, how do policy evaluation, policy improvement, and value iteration use it differently?
V(s) is 4, observed reward is 1, successor value is 6, discount is 0.9, and step size is 0.2. Compute a one-step TD update and explain what is bootstrapped.
Why might Monte Carlo returns be noisy while one-step TD targets can be systematically wrong? How would this affect your method choice?
For rewards 1 and 2, a value estimate of 5 after two steps, and discount 0.9, compute a two-step target. What does increasing the trace parameter lambda change?
An epsilon-greedy policy keeps selecting an action already known to be poor, yet never reaches a useful distant state. What two limitations of naive exploration does this expose?
What distinguishes behavior and target policies in off-policy learning? Why can importance weighting fail when the behavior policy never takes a target action?
For Q(s,a)=2, reward 1, discount 0.9, step size 0.1, and successor action values [4,0] selected by behavior with probabilities [0.8,0.2], compare Expected SARSA with Q-learning.
Why can SARSA learn a safer route near a cliff during epsilon-greedy exploration while Q-learning prefers a shorter risky route?
An off-policy estimator is theoretically unbiased but a few logged trajectories dominate its value estimate. What would you examine before using it for deployment?
Would increasing the number of backups or using longer returns always improve control faster? Separate computational propagation from new evidence.
answers: Policy evaluation backs up expected rewards and successor values under a fixed policy. Policy improvement selects actions using those estimates, giving a better policy under the usual exact-model assumptions. Policy iteration alternates these operations. Value iteration instead uses a maximizing backup during each value update, combining evaluation-like propagation with greedy improvement. A model supplies transition and reward expectations; it does not remove the need to define terminal states, discounting, state coverage, or the objective. Approximation and incomplete convergence can alter the exact guarantees.

The one-step target is 1 + 0.9 × 6 = 6.4, the temporal-difference error is 6.4 − 4 = 2.4, and the updated estimate is 4 + 0.2 × 2.4 = 4.48. The continuation value 6 is a learned prediction rather than a fully observed future return, so the target is bootstrapped. That enables learning before an episode finishes but introduces dependence on current value estimates. Use zero continuation only for genuine termination, not every collection boundary.

Monte Carlo uses the observed remaining return, which can vary substantially with future actions and transitions, and may require waiting until episode completion. One-step TD substitutes a current value estimate for that long sampled tail, reducing sampling dependence but inheriting bootstrap error. Neither label is a universal statement that one method always has less total error. Consider horizon, reward variability, value approximation quality, and data availability. Compare learning behavior and evaluation return rather than selecting solely from training-target variance.

The two-step target is 1 + 0.9 × 2 + 0.9² × 5 = 6.85, assuming no intervening genuine termination. Multi-step targets propagate observed rewards farther before bootstrapping. Lambda mixes backup lengths through traces or lambda returns; increasing it generally places more weight on longer sampled continuations. It does not change the task discount or make rewards beyond a fixed horizon disappear. Check sequence boundaries and behavior-policy assumptions before extending traces across collected fragments.

Uniform random exploration can waste trials on clearly inferior immediate actions instead of directing effort toward uncertain promising actions. Long-horizon exploration can also require a coherent sequence of choices that independent random perturbations almost never produce. A bandit perspective helps reason about uncertainty for immediate decisions, but future-state reachability adds a separate problem. Consider uncertainty-directed methods, demonstrations, structured exploration, or a curriculum appropriate to the task. More random noise alone need not discover the missing rewarding trajectory.

The behavior policy generates the logged experience; the target policy is the one being evaluated or improved. Importance ratios reweight supported action probabilities to correct that difference under specified assumptions. If behavior probability is zero for an action the target might choose, there is no evidence to reweight and the ratio is undefined. Small behavior probabilities can create extreme variance even without exact zeros. Sequential evaluation also involves trajectory or state-distribution effects; a convenient one-step ratio is not a universal correction for every mismatch.

Expected SARSA uses the behavior-policy continuation 0.8 × 4 + 0.2 × 0 = 3.2, giving target 3.88 and update 2 + 0.1 × (3.88 − 2) = 2.188. Q-learning uses the greedy continuation 4, giving target 4.6 and update 2.26. The methods are not just different implementations of the same backup: they evaluate different continuation choices. Ordinary SARSA would use the next action actually sampled rather than its expectation.

SARSA backs up the continuation under the behavior actually used, including the possibility of exploratory actions near the cliff. The expected cost of those future mistakes can favor a safer route. Q-learning uses a greedy continuation target and can prefer the shorter route that would be best under greedy future behavior. This illustrates on-policy versus off-policy targets, not a universal superiority of either method. State the deployed policy, reward penalties, exploration schedule, and task assumptions when interpreting the result.

Inspect support, logged action probabilities, importance-weight distributions, effective sample size, trajectory length, and confidence or sensitivity across seeds and slices. Products of sequential ratios can produce enormous variance, so unbiasedness alone does not establish a useful estimate. Clipping or normalization can reduce variance while introducing bias and should be reported explicitly. If the data do not cover proposed behavior, collect additional evidence or restrict the policy rather than interpreting a fragile point estimate as a deployment guarantee.

Repeated model backups can propagate existing information farther without collecting new transitions, but they depend on the correctness of the model or current estimates. Longer sampled returns propagate observed reward farther per target but can increase variance or require more experience before they are available. Extra computation does not create support for unseen actions or fix a wrong reward function. Compare sample efficiency, wall-clock compute, approximation error, and the task horizon rather than treating more backups or longer targets as uniformly better.

questions: Why can neural off-policy value learning become unstable when function approximation and bootstrapping are combined?
What distinct problems do experience replay and a target network address in a Deep Q-Network?
A DQN transition has reward 2, discount 0.9, and target-network successor action values [3,5]. Compute its target for a continuing transition and for genuine termination.
At the successor state, the online network values are [4,5] and the target network values are [6,2]. With reward 1 and discount 0.9, compare ordinary DQN and Double DQN targets.
Prioritized replay samples high-TD-error transitions more often. Why can that improve learning yet distort the optimization objective?
A value model receives identical camera frames for situations with different velocities and returns inconsistent action values. What changes to representation and replay would you consider?
The DQN TD loss is small and stable, but evaluation return collapses. Which checks come before a bigger network?
Explain why maximizing over noisy action-value estimates can be optimistic even when individual estimates have zero-mean error.
Would an arbitrarily long history always be the best fix for partial observability? What costs and failure modes matter?
An engineer applies a DQN implementation directly to a continuous two-dimensional action space by taking a maximum over its output neurons. What assumption has been violated?
answers: One network shares parameters across many states, so improving one prediction can damage others. Bootstrapped targets depend on current learned predictions rather than fixed labels, and off-policy data may poorly represent the distribution relevant to the target policy. These interacting ingredients can amplify errors instead of contracting them as in a simple tabular setting. Monitor values, TD errors, data coverage, gradients, and evaluation return. A decreasing regression loss does not prove that the induced greedy policy is improving.

Replay reuses stored transitions and breaks some temporal correlation by sampling batches, improving data reuse but also creating an off-policy and potentially stale dataset. A target network provides more slowly changing bootstrap predictions, reducing rapid feedback between the fitted network and its target. Neither fixes unsupported actions, reward mistakes, or all representation instability. Specify replay capacity and sampling, target-update policy, termination masks, and the action-space assumptions rather than treating the two devices as a general convergence guarantee.

For a continuing transition, the DQN target is 2 + 0.9 × max(3,5) = 6.5. For genuine termination it is 2, since no further task return remains. The target is treated as fixed for the current regression update. An external rollout cutoff in a continuing task should generally retain the successor estimate using the final actual observation. Check that the network is not bootstrapping from an automatically reset episode or padded observation.

Ordinary DQN maximizes the target-network values and obtains 1 + 0.9 × 6 = 6.4. Double DQN selects the action with the online network, which chooses the second action, then evaluates that action with the target network, giving 1 + 0.9 × 2 = 2.8. Separating selection and evaluation reduces a source of maximization bias from noisy estimates. It does not guarantee every estimate is unbiased or remove all overestimation in an approximate off-policy system.

High-error transitions may carry useful learning signal, so selective sampling can use updates more efficiently. But changing sampling probabilities changes each record’s expected contribution to the replay objective. Importance weights can correct toward a specified baseline sampling distribution, with practical stabilization often only partially correcting it. Large TD error can also indicate stochastic or mislabeled experience rather than useful novelty. Compare evaluation return, coverage, weight variance, and replay diversity instead of assuming the highest-error examples are always best.

The current frame may not contain enough state information. Add a meaningful frame stack, recurrent memory, or a state estimator that can infer motion. For recurrent training, replay contiguous sequences with correct masks, episode boundaries, and sufficient history or burn-in to construct the hidden state; randomly isolated transitions may not reproduce that state. Avoid leaking future observations that are unavailable at action time. Test whether the added history resolves ambiguity rather than only increasing model capacity.

Verify reward scale and sign, action mapping, termination/truncation handling, successor observations, loss-target detachment, and evaluation policy. Inspect state/action coverage, Q-value magnitudes, replay age, target-network updates, and whether a few actions are spuriously overvalued. A small residual can reflect fitting self-consistent but wrong bootstrap targets. Reproduce a tiny known task and compare actual returns with value predictions. Capacity changes should follow evidence of representation underfit, not substitute for validating the learning pipeline.

The maximum preferentially selects actions with positive estimation noise. Averaging an individual action’s error before selection is different from selecting the largest noisy estimate and then averaging its value. More candidate actions can increase that selection effect. Double estimators reduce the coupling by choosing with one estimate and evaluating with another, though correlated estimates and function approximation limit the ideal benefit. Distinguish this estimation bias from genuine high expected return or deliberate exploration bonuses.

Longer history can reveal hidden state, but adds storage, compute, credit-assignment difficulty, and sensitivity to irrelevant or stale observations. Recurrence compresses history and can forget necessary evidence or receive an incorrect hidden state during replay. Choose a history representation from the dynamics and information needed for action selection, then compare against simple stacks or measured state features. Evaluate across resets, delayed observations, and realistic deployment timing rather than assuming more context always improves decisions.

A standard DQN has a finite set of output action values, making the greedy maximum an enumeration over discrete actions. A continuous action vector cannot be represented as that same finite action index without an explicit discretization policy and its approximation costs. Check action dimensionality, bounds, resolution, and whether a parameterized actor or another continuous-control method is appropriate. Increasing the number of output neurons does not by itself define the mapping or make exhaustive search over continuous actions valid.

questions: Why does a policy-gradient estimator multiply a return or advantage by the gradient of log action probability, rather than differentiating the environment reward directly?
Why can subtracting an action-independent state baseline reduce policy-gradient variance without changing its expectation? What changes when the advantage is bootstrapped?
For TD errors 1 and 2, discount 0.9, and GAE parameter lambda 0.8, compute the first two-step generalized advantage estimate. Does changing lambda change the task discount?
PPO uses min(rA, clip(r,0.8,1.2)A). Evaluate it for r=1.5, A=2 and for r=0.5, A=−2. Why must the sign of advantage be considered?
A PPO implementation reuses the same rollout for many epochs until its training objective improves, while policy KL and evaluation performance deteriorate. What would you inspect?
For continuous control, what are the distinct jobs of a deterministic actor and a critic? Why does the actor update depend on the critic’s derivative with respect to action?

An off-policy actor–critic uses the smaller of two successor Q estimates, 8 and 5. With reward 1 and discount 0.9, compute the target. If an entropy term uses alpha=0.2 and log probability −1, what is the corresponding soft target?
Why might maximizing expected reward plus entropy help continuous-control learning? Why can increasing the entropy coefficient too much harm the task?
Actor and critic share an encoder. The critic loss drops sharply, but policy quality worsens. Why is independently checking the actor head insufficient?
How would discrete versus continuous actions and available replay data influence choosing a value-based method, an on-policy policy-gradient method, or an off-policy actor–critic?
answers: The score-function identity differentiates the probability of sampling an action or trajectory. Weighting the log-probability gradient by its learning signal increases probability for outcomes that were better than expected, without requiring differentiable environment dynamics. The return or advantage is normally treated as a fixed signal in that actor update. State the objective and sampling assumptions: arbitrary old trajectories require appropriate off-policy handling, and shared value or reward models do not make every dependency part of the intended actor gradient.

For a fixed state, the expected score gradient is the gradient of the sum of action probabilities, which is zero. Multiplying by an action-independent baseline preserves that zero expectation, so subtracting the baseline from a complete sampled return does not change the expected actor gradient under the usual conditions. Treat it as fixed in that calculation. A bootstrapped advantage is different: it replaces part of the sampled future with a learned continuation estimate and can introduce bias through critic error. An arbitrary action-dependent baseline needs a correction.

The estimate is 1 + (0.9 × 0.8) × 2 = 2.44. With lambda zero it would use just the first TD error, 1. Lambda controls the mixture of error horizons used by the estimator; gamma still specifies how task rewards are discounted. Stop recursion at relevant sequence boundaries and bootstrap a continuing rollout’s final observation correctly. Do not let the trace spill into the reset episode or claim that a larger lambda guarantees a better critic or a lower-variance estimate.

For positive advantage, min(3, 2.4) = 2.4. For negative advantage, min(−1, −1.6) = −1.6. The minimum chooses a pessimistic improvement surrogate relative to the clipping interval; clipping is not simply replacing every ratio with a bounded value regardless of sign. These are per-sample objective values, normally maximized or negated for a loss. The clipped surrogate reduces some incentives for large probability changes, but is not a hard guarantee that every action probability or the full policy divergence remains within a fixed trust region.

Check that old-policy log probabilities are fixed from collection and ratios use the intended actions and masks. Measure policy divergence, clipping fraction, advantage and value scales, entropy, learning rate, and epoch/minibatch reuse. Excessive optimization on one rollout can move the policy beyond a useful local update even with clipping. Consider fewer epochs, a smaller step, or a KL-based stopping policy, then collect fresh experience. A better surrogate on old data does not prove improved on-policy return.

The actor maps a state to an action; the critic estimates return for a state/action pair. Instead of enumerating continuous actions, the actor changes its parameters to produce actions the critic rates more highly, using the chain rule through the action into Q. The critic is fitted to a bootstrapped return target, while its parameters are held fixed for the intended actor update. Critic extrapolation error can therefore directly mislead the actor. Action bounds, scaling, target networks, and exploration behavior must be consistent.

Without the entropy term, the clipped-double-Q target is 1 + 0.9 × 5 = 5.5 for a continuing transition. With the soft continuation min Q − alpha × log probability, it becomes 1 + 0.9 × (5 − 0.2 × (−1)) = 5.68. The negative log probability makes entropy contribute positively in this convention. Specify the exact objective and terminal masking rather than swapping signs from memory. Twin critics help control overestimation but do not eliminate unsupported-action or function-approximation errors.

An entropy bonus rewards a broader action distribution as well as task return, encouraging exploration and avoiding premature collapse onto one brittle action choice. Its coefficient sets a genuine objective tradeoff, not just numerical regularization. Too much weight can keep behavior unnecessarily random and reduce useful task performance; too little can collapse exploration. Interpret the coefficient relative to reward scaling and the policy distribution, and evaluate the actual deployment behavior rather than assuming more stochasticity is always safer or more effective.

The critic’s gradients also change the shared representation, potentially harming features used by the actor. Inspect loss weighting, gradient scales, target validity, advantage detachment, optimization schedules, and whether recent critic data are too narrow. An imperfect baseline alone need not bias a full-return score estimator, but an inaccurate bootstrapped advantage can mislead it. Compare separate encoders or controlled critic-update ratios when evidence points to interference. Head-only checks miss changes upstream of both outputs.

A discrete value model can enumerate action values and use replay when its assumptions fit. Policy-gradient methods directly parameterize behavior and can handle stochastic or continuous choices, but typical on-policy updates need fresh rollout data. Off-policy actor–critics can reuse continuous-control experience and avoid exhaustive action maximization, at the cost of critic errors and distribution mismatch. Start from action structure, interaction cost, observation quality, and a simple baseline. Do not choose an algorithm solely because one benchmark reports higher final return.

questions: A learned dynamics model has low one-step prediction error but produces poor long simulated rollouts. Why can planning exploit its mistakes?
When can model-based planning be worth its complexity compared with learning a policy directly?
Behavior cloning has high validation accuracy on expert data but fails after a small mistake online. What distribution shift is occurring, and how might additional data help?
Why does maximizing a learned Q function over actions become especially risky in offline RL, even if fitted value loss is small?
When is behavior cloning a useful baseline for offline RL, and what does offline RL try to add?
In a one-step bandit, behavior chooses two actions equally, the target probabilities are [0.75,0.25], and deterministic rewards are [4,0]. Compute expected importance-weighted reward.
A new policy looks excellent under logged-data evaluation, but its improvement is driven by actions with tiny behavior probabilities. How would you challenge the conclusion?
How does learning from preference comparisons differ from having an environment-defined reward, and why can optimizing a reward model become misleading?
In a tool-using language agent, what are the state, action, transition, and reward? Why is next-token prediction loss alone insufficient to evaluate the agent?
A policy’s verifier-based reward rises because it learns a shortcut in the checker, while human-rated success drops. What do you change first?
answers: Small one-step errors accumulate as predicted states become inputs for later predictions. Planning may also search for actions or states where the model is confidently wrong, especially outside observed support. Low average one-step error on logged data does not establish reliable counterfactual trajectories. Compare imagined and real outcomes across relevant horizons and slices, use uncertainty or short planning horizons where justified, and validate proposed behavior in the environment. More search can amplify model bias instead of correcting it.

Planning can reuse a learned or known model to compare future actions, improve sample efficiency, and adapt to changed goals without collecting every full trajectory again. Its value depends on model accuracy in relevant regions, branching/action complexity, available inference time, and the cost of real interactions. A wrong model can bias decisions even when search is thorough. Compare a model-free or simple reactive baseline under equal environment and compute budgets, and measure the latency cost of planning at deployment.

Supervised validation measures predictions on the expert’s state distribution. The learned policy’s mistakes can move it to unfamiliar states, where further errors compound and the expert dataset supplies no corrective actions. Collect expert corrections or aggregate demonstrations at states visited by the learner when feasible, rather than only repeating expert trajectories. Also inspect observation and action alignment, label ambiguity, and coverage. More supervised training on the same narrow expert distribution does not necessarily repair rollout behavior.

The fixed dataset may contain little or no evidence for some actions. Maximization can select an unsupported action with an overestimated Q value, and bootstrapping can reinforce that error without new interaction to correct it. Small loss on logged actions does not validate counterfactual actions. Offline methods therefore constrain behavior toward supported actions or penalize overly optimistic values, with explicit tradeoffs between improvement and conservatism. Check dataset support, policy shift, and evaluation uncertainty before trusting the greedy policy.

Behavior cloning asks the model to imitate observed actions, providing a simple supervised baseline that can work well when demonstrations are high quality and adequately cover deployment states. Offline RL attempts to improve reward-based decisions using a fixed experience dataset, potentially combining good segments or preferring better observed behavior. That requires reward and support assumptions beyond imitation. Compare on held-out tasks with uncertainty-aware evaluation; a more elaborate offline algorithm is not justified merely because it optimizes a Q-based objective.

The action ratios are 0.75/0.5 = 1.5 and 0.25/0.5 = 0.5. Averaging over behavior gives 0.5 × 1.5 × 4 + 0.5 × 0.5 × 0 = 3, matching the target’s direct expected reward. This example assumes known accurate propensities and support for both actions. Sequential trajectory ratios and noisy finite samples introduce further variance and coverage issues. The training critic’s own predicted return is not an independent off-policy evaluation of that same policy.

Inspect action support, propensity validity, weight tails, effective sample size, estimator sensitivity, and uncertainty by relevant slice. Check whether the proposed policy visits states not represented by the logged behavior. Compare direct-model, importance-based, and corrected estimators without interpreting agreement as proof when they share data or misspecification. Restrict unsupported changes or collect new evidence where possible. A point estimate dominated by a few high-weight records is weak evidence for deployment, especially when rare adverse outcomes matter.

Preferences supply relative judgments under a particular annotation process, not automatically a calibrated task reward. A reward model learns a proxy and can reflect annotator bias, noise, and incomplete coverage. Strong policy optimization may exploit weaknesses in that proxy, increasing predicted reward while reducing usefulness or safety. Validate on held-out comparisons and independent task outcomes, monitor distribution shift, and control the update strength. Direct preference objectives and online policy optimization use different data and optimization mechanisms even when both consume comparisons.

The state or observation includes the current conversation and available environment information; actions may be generated tokens or executable tool requests. Tool results and other environment changes produce transitions, while reward can reflect verified task success, costs, and constraints. Token likelihood measures fit to text targets, not whether the sequence of decisions achieved the external goal. Define the actual action granularity, observability, delayed credit, and verification process. Evaluate completed tasks and invalid or costly actions under the deployed loop.

Treat the discrepancy as an objective and measurement problem before changing the optimizer. Inspect the rewarded behaviors, checker assumptions, reward decomposition, and examples where verifier success disagrees with the task. Strengthen or independently validate outcome verification, use held-out cases, and retain constraints or cost metrics that reward alone misses. Further optimization against the same flawed checker can worsen exploitation. Compare performance using evidence that was not itself the optimization target.

questions: A navigation agent gets a small reward for approaching a goal but learns to move back and forth near it. Why is training reward not enough to establish success?
Potential-based shaping adds gamma Φ(s′) − Φ(s). With gamma=0.9, Φ(s)=−3, and Φ(s′)=−2, compute the bonus. Why do terminal conventions matter for policy invariance?
A successful outcome occurs only after a long coordinated action sequence. Which evidence distinguishes a learning-rule bug from an exploration bottleneck?
Adding more environment actors increases transitions/second but worsens return per environment step. What policy-lag and data-quality issues would you examine?
Run A reaches a target after 1 million environment steps in two hours. Run B needs 2 million steps but reaches it in one hour using more workers. Which is more sample-efficient and which is faster?
An RL run’s loss curves look smooth, yet the policy repeatedly chooses one action and fails a tiny task. What would your first debugging pass include?
You report the best-performing seed after tuning hyperparameters on the same five evaluation tasks. Why can the deployment estimate be optimistic?
A control policy scores well in simulation but fails on real hardware. Which gaps would you test before concluding the algorithm itself is wrong?
How would you choose a baseline and deployment plan for a continuous-control policy trained mostly from demonstrations and simulation?
What measurements would you require to compare two RL methods fairly if one uses more demonstrations, more simulator resets, and more tuning?
answers: The agent optimizes the reward actually implemented, which may repeatedly pay for a proxy without completing the goal. Inspect reward components, episode boundaries, state information, and actual trajectories. Measure independent success, time, and constraint violations rather than only total training reward. Redesign the proxy or use a theoretically justified shaping term with correct terminal handling when its assumptions apply. More capacity or exploration can make exploitation of the same incorrect objective stronger.

The bonus is 0.9 × (−2) − (−3) = 1.2. Under the appropriate discounted-task conditions, shaping terms telescope, leaving a state-dependent offset rather than arbitrarily changing action preferences. The remaining terminal-potential term must be handled consistently, commonly using zero terminal potential for finite episodes. Incorrect resets, truncation treatment, or changing the task objective can break that argument. A positive shaping bonus on one transition is not by itself evidence that a policy has improved its original task return.

Check whether any rewarding trajectories enter the dataset and whether the learner can reproduce or improve supplied successful experience in a small controlled test. If success is never observed, a correct update has no useful task signal to exploit. Consider demonstrations, a curriculum, structured exploration, or suitable shaping instead of only increasing random action noise. Also inspect reward delivery, reset conditions, and horizon. Diagnose discovery and credit propagation separately; both can fail in long tasks for different reasons.

Asynchronous actors may collect under older policies while the learner changes rapidly, creating more off-policy experience than the update can handle. Inspect policy version lag, replay age, rollout lengths, reset behavior, observation/action preprocessing, and learner-to-environment update ratio. Raw transition rate can also hide duplicated or invalid data. Compare sample efficiency, wall-clock time to a quality target, and resource cost. Faster collection is useful only when the learning method can use that distribution and the evaluation behavior improves.

Run A is more sample-efficient because it uses half as many environment interactions to achieve the same target. Run B is faster in wall-clock time, taking one rather than two hours. Resource efficiency cannot be decided without worker counts, costs, and other compute. If real interactions are expensive or constrained, the extra samples may dominate; if simulation is cheap and latency matters, the faster run may be preferable. Keep the target metric, evaluation conditions, and seed variability consistent before comparing.

Verify action indices and bounds, observation normalization, reward sign, episode reset, termination masks, successor-state handling, and exploration configuration. Inspect actual trajectories, action probabilities or Q values, gradient flow, target detachment, and policy/optimizer updates. Try a small known environment and a simple baseline, then isolate collection, storage, targets, and learning separately. Smooth losses can describe a self-consistent but broken pipeline; they are not evidence of useful control or successful exploration.

Selecting a favorable seed and repeatedly tuning on the evaluation tasks makes the reported result a selection statistic rather than an independent performance estimate. Use a separate tuning process and held-out tasks or conditions, report variation across multiple seeds, and state the environment and action-selection policy. Look at failures and distribution slices as well as average return. More evaluation episodes on the same selected tasks may reduce sampling noise while leaving task-selection overfitting intact.

Compare sensor and action latency, observation noise, dynamics parameters, contact or actuator behavior, action bounds, reset distributions, and reward measurement. A simulator may omit constraints or rare cases that materially affect control. Test robust performance across parameter and observation variations and validate low-risk deployment behavior with appropriate fallback. Sim-to-real failure can arise from model or interface mismatch even when the learning rule is implemented correctly. Separate generalization evidence from performance on the training simulator.

Start from the task, action bounds, observation availability, interaction cost, and meaningful success/constraint metrics. Compare a simple controller and behavior-cloning baseline before more complex RL. Validate simulator and demonstration coverage, use held-out conditions and repeated evaluations, and check the exact observation/action pipeline used at deployment. Roll out with bounded actions, monitored outcomes, fallback behavior, and explicit versioning. Choose additional RL complexity only when it improves evidence relevant to the actual task and operating constraints.

Report the sources and amount of interaction data, demonstration access, reset privileges, environment difficulty, tuning budget, compute, and evaluation procedure. Compare both sample and wall-clock efficiency at consistent quality targets, with repeated seeds and held-out tasks. A method given expert trajectories or privileged observations is solving a different information problem from one learning unaided. Make those differences explicit rather than attributing all performance to the named algorithm or selecting only its most favorable run.

questions: What information can a waveform carry about linguistic content, speaker identity, prosody, and the recording channel? Why should these not be treated as interchangeable labels?
How many samples and raw payload bytes are in two seconds of 16-kHz, mono, 16-bit PCM audio? What changes if the same recording has two channels?
A 12-kHz tone is sampled at 16 kHz. What alias can appear, and why is changing the sample-rate metadata not equivalent to resampling audio?
At 16 kHz, a 400-point transform has what bin spacing? If you zero-pad a 400-sample window to 512 points, what improves and what does not?
Using valid unpadded frames, how many STFT frames come from 16,000 samples with window length 400 and hop 160? State frame and hop durations at 16 kHz.
How would you choose between longer windows and smaller hops for distinguishing nearby harmonics versus localizing short events?
Why are log-Mel features common for speech recognition, and what information do they discard compared with a waveform or complex spectrogram?
A model performs well on close-talk recordings but fails in a reverberant room. Would peak-normalizing every clip remove the mismatch?
An offline audio pipeline uses centered STFT frames and normalization over the complete utterance, then is deployed as a low-latency stream. Where can unavailable future information enter?
Would increasing sample rate and retaining a raw waveform always improve an audio ML system compared with a compact feature representation?
answers: A waveform combines speech production with speaker characteristics, timing and intonation, background sources, room acoustics, and microphone effects. A recognizer targets linguistic content, while a speaker model should preserve identity and become less sensitive to some content or channel changes. Prosody and acoustic events can matter for other tasks. Define which factors are signal and which are nuisance for the objective. A representation useful for one target may intentionally discard information another target requires.

There are 16,000 × 2 = 32,000 samples per channel. Sixteen bits means two bytes per sample, giving 64,000 payload bytes for mono audio. Two channels double that to 128,000 bytes, before headers or container overhead. Sample rate describes the time grid; sample precision describes representable amplitudes; channel count describes simultaneous streams. A neural tensor may later store samples as 32-bit floating point, so its in-memory size need not equal the PCM file payload.

The Nyquist frequency is 8 kHz, so 12 kHz cannot be represented unambiguously; it aliases to 4 kHz under this example. Proper downsampling requires filtering out unsupported frequencies before selecting a coarser time grid. Simply relabeling existing samples changes their interpreted duration and pitch rather than reconstructing a valid resampled waveform. Check the recording rate, model frontend rate, and preprocessing path instead of interpreting the resulting artifacts as a recognition-model capacity problem.

The 400-point bin spacing is 16,000/400 = 40 Hz. A 512-point transform samples the spectrum on a finer grid, 16,000/512 = 31.25 Hz. Zero-padding does not add observed time or make two close tones fundamentally more distinguishable than the original window supports; it interpolates the spectral representation. Frequency discrimination depends on observation length and window shape as well as the displayed grid. Distinguish true resolution from prettier or denser frequency bins.

The count is 1 + floor((16,000 − 400)/160) = 98 frames. The window lasts 400/16,000 = 25 milliseconds, and the hop is 160/16,000 = 10 milliseconds.
