Centering or boundary padding can produce a different frame count, so specify those conventions before comparing tensor shapes. A 10-millisecond hop does not mean each frame uses only 10 milliseconds of audio or eliminates the time smearing introduced by the 25-millisecond window.

Longer windows use more observation time and can distinguish close frequency components better, but blend rapid temporal changes. Smaller hops provide more frequent overlapping measurements, improving sampling of feature evolution without undoing the window’s temporal smoothing. Both choices affect frame count, compute, and downstream context cost. Evaluate the task’s time and frequency scales, frontend compatibility, and streaming delay instead of assuming the highest-resolution-looking spectrogram is always the best model input.

Mel filterbanks combine spectral energy into perceptually motivated frequency bands; logarithms compress dynamic range and make relative energy differences easier to model. This can provide a compact useful input for linguistic prediction. Filterbank compression loses fine spectral detail, and common magnitude/power features omit phase, so inversion is not unique. Cepstral transforms further reorganize or truncate information. A frontend chosen for recognition is not automatically sufficient for exact waveform reconstruction, speaker cues, or every acoustic event.

Peak normalization changes amplitude scale but does not remove room impulse responses, overlapping sources, microphone frequency response, clipping, or timing differences. It may also erase amplitude cues relevant to the task. Inspect channel conditions and actual recordings, compare matched preprocessing, and consider realistic reverberation/noise augmentation or adaptation. Validate which variation should be invariant for the target. Treating every shift as loudness can hide the acoustic mechanism that caused the failure.

A centered frame can require samples after its nominal timestamp, and whole-utterance normalization uses statistics that are unavailable before the utterance ends. A bidirectional model or later preprocessing can add further future context. Specify the actual timestamp and available lookahead at every stage, then use a causal or deliberately bounded-lookahead frontend with matching training. Reducing inference compute alone does not make these dependencies streamable. Measure first usable and final output delay under real chunk arrivals.

Higher sample rate and raw input can preserve information but increase bandwidth, storage, model work, and the burden of learning useful invariances. Extra high-frequency content may be irrelevant or absent in the deployment channel. Compact features can improve data efficiency but discard phase or fine detail important for some tasks. Choose from the target, recording conditions, available data, model architecture, and latency constraints. Compare controlled end-to-end quality and resource use rather than only input dimensionality.

questions: A classifier assigns probabilities [0.7,0.2,0.1] and the correct class is the first. What is cross-entropy loss for this example? How does it change if correct-class probability falls to 0.1?
Training loss and validation loss both stay high on a small audio classification task. Would stronger regularization be your first response?
Two temporal convolutions have kernel/stride pairs (5,2) then (3,2), with no padding or dilation. What are the effective stride and receptive field in input samples?
Why can temporal subsampling improve an audio encoder’s efficiency while harming recognition or event timing?
What do recurrent models and attention-based encoders contribute beyond independent frame classification for variable-length audio?
A padded batch produces different predictions for the same utterance depending on the lengths of other examples. What masks and normalization choices would you inspect?
If sequence length doubles while hidden width and head dimensions remain fixed, how does dense attention’s token-pair count change? Does a convolution–attention hybrid automatically become causal?
How can self-supervised audio pretraining help when transcripts are scarce, and why does it not eliminate the need for task-specific validation?
An augmentation that helps speech-content recognition hurts speaker verification. Why might that be expected rather than evidence that the augmentation implementation is broken?
For a rare audio event, why can high overall accuracy coexist with a useless detector? Which model and evaluation decisions follow?
answers: With a one-hot target, cross-entropy is the negative natural logarithm of the correct-class probability. It is −log(0.7), approximately 0.357, and becomes −log(0.1), approximately 2.303. Confidently assigning low probability to the true label is strongly penalized. The full distribution must still be normalized; if a library expects logits, do not mistakenly apply a second softmax to probabilities. For variable-length audio, define which frames or tokens contribute and how the loss is normalized.

Not without evidence. First check labels, frontend shapes and scaling, loss/output compatibility, masks, gradient flow, learning rate, and whether the model can overfit a tiny clean subset. High training error suggests underfitting or an optimization/data problem rather than ordinary overfitting. Stronger regularization can worsen it. Compare a simple baseline and inspect actual inputs before adding architecture complexity. When training fit improves but held-out performance deteriorates, investigate generalization and leakage separately.

The effective stride is 2 × 2 = 4 input samples per final output position. The receptive field is 5 + (3 − 1) × 2 = 9 input samples: the second layer spans three first-layer outputs whose centers are two input samples apart. Channel count does not change this temporal footprint. Translate the result to time using the input sample or feature-frame rate, and check padding and lookahead conventions before inferring streaming latency or alignment feasibility.

Subsampling reduces the number of time positions processed downstream, potentially lowering recurrent work and the quadratic pair count of dense attention. But it also reduces temporal resolution and may erase brief events or leave too few encoder positions for a target alignment. The receptive field and causality of the subsampling layers matter too. Compare compute savings with label timing, short-utterance behavior, and the requirements of the selected sequence objective rather than maximizing stride blindly.

They use relationships across time to interpret ambiguous local evidence and produce context-sensitive representations. A recurrent model carries a hidden state; attention directly combines selected positions subject to masks and context limits. Variable lengths require correct padding masks, state resets, and output lengths. Bidirectional context can help offline quality but requires future audio, while causal or bounded-context alternatives trade information for streamability. Independent frame labels are appropriate only when the target and available context support that simplification.

Verify true lengths, attention key masks, loss masks, recurrent packing or state handling, and any normalization that uses batch or time statistics. Padded values should not contribute as genuine audio or targets. Incorrect masks can let the model attend to padding, while a batch-dependent normalization can legitimately change behavior with batch composition unless designed otherwise. Compare an utterance alone with the same utterance in padded batches and localize the first mismatching layer. Do not assume zeros are intrinsically ignored.

The number of query–key pairs grows from T² to (2T)² = 4T², so that component has approximately four times the pairwise work and naive score storage. Projections and feed-forward work need not scale by the same factor. A hybrid encoder is causal only if attention masks, convolutions, normalization, and other context dependencies respect the available past or stated lookahead. Combining a convolution with attention does not by itself determine streamability.

A pretext objective learns useful representations from unlabeled recordings, such as predicting masked content or distinguishing related views. Fine-tuning can then use fewer task labels than learning all structure from scratch. The pretrained model still reflects its data, objective, frontend, and context assumptions, which may differ from the deployment domain. Validate on the target task with appropriate speaker/session splits and compare frozen and adapted baselines. More pretraining data does not automatically provide calibrated labels or robust behavior under a new channel.

Augmentations encode assumptions about which changes should preserve the label. A transformation that preserves words can alter pitch, timbre, or other identity cues needed for speaker verification. Conversely, retaining channel cues may spuriously help identify speakers in one dataset while harming generalization. Inspect label semantics, augmentation strength, and task-specific validation, rather than transferring a successful recipe unchanged. Positive and negative pairs in self-supervised learning must also reflect the desired invariances.

A model predicting no event can achieve high accuracy when negatives dominate while missing most true events. Examine precision, recall, relevant thresholds, false activations per unit time, and the cost of missed events. Match a multilabel or multiclass output and loss to the actual label structure, and use validation distributions representative of deployment. Class weighting or sampling can help learning but may affect calibration. A threshold should be chosen from the service objective, not assumed to be 0.5.

questions: How would choosing characters, wordpieces, or words as recognition targets affect vocabulary coverage, output length, and training data requirements?
An ASR dataset mixes punctuation, capitalization, and spoken-versus-written number conventions. How can this create apparently inconsistent errors?
In CTC, collapse the path [a,a,blank,a]. Why does removing blanks before merging repeats give a different and incorrect interpretation?
A two-frame CTC model has P(a)=0.4 and P(blank)=0.6 at both frames. What transcript does greedy path decoding produce, and what is the total probability of transcript a?
The CTC target is book, four labels with one adjacent repeated pair. Can an encoder with only four valid time positions represent it? What would you inspect if the loss is infinite?
What conditional independence does the CTC path factorization assume, and why is it wrong to say that CTC requires statistically independent audio frames?
Compare CTC, an RNN-transducer, and an attention encoder–decoder for alignment, output-label dependence, and streaming.
A model trained with a streaming transducer objective still waits for the full utterance before emitting useful output. What could explain the delay?
Why can beam search and an external language model improve recognition, and how can their scoring weights damage rare or acoustically clear words?
Contextual biasing improves recognition of contact names but inserts those names into unrelated speech. How would you tune and evaluate it?
answers: Characters provide broad spelling coverage but produce longer sequences and leave more linguistic structure to the model or decoder. Wordpieces balance sequence length and compositional coverage, with behavior depending on the tokenizer and training text. Whole words shorten common outputs but enlarge the vocabulary and have explicit rare/unseen-word limitations unless supplemented. Compare the language, script, data, alignment objective, and decoding constraints. Changing target units also changes sequence lengths and error interpretation, so token accuracy across tokenizers is not directly comparable.

The same acoustic content can map to different label strings depending on transcript normalization. A model may be penalized for a reasonable alternative that disagrees with inconsistent annotation conventions, and decoder bias can favor one style. Define the target written form, text normalization, tokenizer, and scoring rules consistently across train and evaluation. Inspect examples rather than labeling all mismatches acoustic failures. If formatting is a separate product requirement, evaluate it explicitly instead of silently changing the recognition metric.

CTC first merges consecutive repeated labels, giving [a,blank,a], and then removes blanks, giving the transcript aa. Removing the blank first would create adjacent a labels and collapse them to a single a, losing the repeated output. Blank is an alignment symbol, not necessarily silence or a word boundary. The model’s transcript probability sums all paths obeying the correct collapse rule, so a mistaken implementation changes both decoding and the set of alignments associated with a target.

The highest-probability label at each frame is blank, so greedy path decoding produces the empty transcript with path probability 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36. Transcript a has three paths: [a,blank], [blank,a], and [a,a]. Their probabilities sum to 0.24 + 0.24 + 0.16 = 0.64. Thus the most probable path need not collapse to the most probable transcript. CTC-aware beam search aggregates compatible path mass rather than simply treating every emitted label sequence as an independent ordinary text hypothesis.

The repeated o labels need a separating blank, so the minimum number of valid positions is U + R = 4 + 1 = 5. Four valid positions cannot produce this target under the collapse rule. Check true encoder lengths after subsampling, target tokenization, repeated-label counts, padding masks, and blank placement. Infinite loss can represent an impossible alignment rather than ordinary gradient instability. Suppressing infinite losses may keep a run numerically alive while silently discarding the problematic examples.

Given the encoded input, CTC factors a path’s label probabilities over time positions. Its output head does not explicitly condition each emitted label on the previously emitted label sequence. The encoder can nevertheless use substantial temporal context and produce representations dependent on many audio frames. The assumption concerns the path-label factorization, not independence of the observed waveform. This distinction explains why CTC can use powerful context encoders yet benefit from label-dependent alternatives or external language-model decoding.

CTC marginalizes monotonic frame-label paths with a blank and a comparatively simple label factorization. A transducer combines an acoustic encoder, label-history prediction, and joint scoring, allowing variable label emissions with monotonic progression. An attention encoder–decoder conditions on previous outputs and can attend over encoded audio, with different alignment and context assumptions. Streaming depends on encoder context, attention constraints, and inference policy, not just the objective name. Compare data, decoding complexity, latency, and error behavior rather than declaring one architecture universally best.

The encoder or frontend may require future context despite the objective’s monotonic structure. Emission timing, blank preference, chunk policy, batching, decoder scheduling, and endpointing can add delay even with a causal encoder. Measure when audio becomes available and when stable partial or final text is emitted. Inspect context dependencies and actual alignment timing before focusing only on kernel speed. Training with a streaming-compatible objective does not guarantee low end-to-end user latency.

Beam search explores alternatives beyond a locally best path, while a language model contributes textual plausibility not fully captured by the acoustic model. Combined scores often need calibrated weights and length or insertion handling. Excessive linguistic preference can replace acoustically supported rare words with common ones, bias transcript length, or amplify a domain mismatch. Tune on representative validation data and inspect substitutions, deletions, and insertions. Keep the recognition objective and language-model contribution distinct when diagnosing improvements.

The context prior may be overpowering acoustic evidence or broadening hypotheses too aggressively. Measure name recall together with false insertions, overall word error, unrelated-utterance behavior, and latency under realistic context-list sizes. Adjust bias strength and triggering conditions using held-out examples, including cases where no listed term is spoken. Context should help resolve ambiguity, not force a match. Test changing or noisy contact lists rather than evaluating only recordings known to contain a target name.

questions: How do clip-level audio classification, temporal event detection, and keyword spotting differ in their outputs and error costs?
A keyword detector has 99% accuracy on a balanced clip dataset but repeatedly triggers on background audio in deployment. What evaluation and threshold changes are needed?

A verification system falsely accepts 30 of 10,000 impostor trials and rejects 20 of 1,000 genuine trials. Compute false-accept and false-reject rates. What happens when its similarity acceptance threshold is lowered?
Two speaker embeddings are [3,4] and [0,5]. Compute cosine similarity. Why should that number not automatically be interpreted as an 80% probability of identity match?
What does speaker diarization answer that automatic speech recognition and voice activity detection do not? Why is speaker identity not necessarily a known real-world name?

Under a scoring convention with nonoverlapping error counts, diarization has 3 seconds missed speech, 2 seconds false speech, and 5 seconds speaker confusion over 40 seconds reference speaker time. What is DER?
How do denoising, source separation, and acoustic echo cancellation differ? Why can a perceptually cleaner signal reduce recognition accuracy?
A two-speaker separator returns accurate sources in swapped output order and receives a large supervised loss. What is the target-assignment problem?
How can paired audio and text train a shared retrieval space, and why is retrieval quality not the same as transcript accuracy?
An audio embedding model performs well when recordings from the same session appear in train and test, but poorly on new microphones. What shortcut and data-split problems would you investigate?
answers: Clip classification identifies which categories occur in a recording, often with multiple labels. Event detection additionally localizes when events occur, so onset/offset accuracy and overlapping labels matter. Keyword spotting recognizes a specific trigger under constraints such as continuous operation, false activations, and response delay. Match labels, pooling, loss, and scoring to that output. A high clip-level score does not prove timely detection, and a threshold acceptable on balanced test clips can generate too many false triggers in long mostly-negative streams.

Evaluate representative continuous negative audio and report false activations per hour together with miss rate and trigger delay. Clip accuracy on an artificial class balance does not capture deployment prevalence, repeated opportunities to trigger, or long correlated noise. Include hard negatives, realistic microphones and environments, and choose the operating threshold on validation data for the actual false-alarm budget. Check event aggregation, cooldown, and endpoint rules, since repeated correlated frame positives need not correspond to independent user-visible activations.

The false-accept rate is 30/10,000 = 0.3%, and the false-reject rate is 20/1,000 = 2%. Lowering a threshold that accepts higher similarity scores generally accepts more trials: false rejects decrease while false accepts increase. These rates condition on different trial types, so do not use one combined denominator. Select the operating point using realistic enrollment and channel conditions and the application’s error costs; equal-error rate is a comparison convention, not automatically the correct deployment threshold.

Their dot product is 20 and both norms are 5, so cosine similarity is 20/25 = 0.8. It is a geometric score, not a calibrated posterior probability. Match probabilities depend on score distributions, training objective, enrollment conditions, channel variation, and prior prevalence. Validate thresholds or calibration on representative genuine and impostor trials, including unseen speakers as appropriate. Distinguish identification among known speakers from verification of a claimed identity; they impose different decisions and evaluation protocols.

Diarization determines who spoke when, commonly assigning anonymous speaker labels to time intervals. Voice activity detection locates speech versus nonspeech, and recognition produces linguistic content; neither alone assigns consistent speaker turns. Diarization can use embeddings, segmentation, clustering, and overlap handling. Speaker labels need not identify a named person unless a separate enrollment or identification process is provided. Evaluate missed speech, false speech, and speaker confusion with explicit overlap and boundary conventions rather than substituting transcript quality for diarization quality.

The diarization error rate is (3 + 2 + 5)/40 = 0.25, or 25%, under the stated convention. The denominator is scored reference speaker time, not blindly the recording’s wall-clock duration. Overlap handling, scoring collars near boundaries, and label matching can change the reported result. Specify these before comparing systems. A lower total can also hide worse speaker confusion or missed speech, so inspect components and representative conversations as well as the aggregate rate.

Denoising suppresses unwanted noise relative to a target; separation estimates distinct sources; echo cancellation removes a known playback signal’s acoustic return. Their available inputs and desired outputs differ. Processing can introduce artifacts or remove speech cues needed by a downstream recognizer even when human listeners prefer the result. Evaluate both signal/perceptual measures and the actual downstream task under matched conditions. Do not assume one enhancement stage benefits recognition, speaker verification, and event detection equally.

The physical sources do not necessarily have a canonical output ordering. Comparing output one with reference one and output two with reference two can penalize an otherwise correct separation solely for swapping channels. Use a loss or matching procedure that evaluates the relevant source permutations, while maintaining a consistent strategy for tracking across chunks when needed. This is distinct from ignoring speaker identity: downstream diarization or targeted extraction may impose additional identity constraints beyond unordered separation.

A contrastive objective can bring matching audio/text representations together and push sampled nonmatches apart. Retrieval then ranks candidates by a learned similarity rather than necessarily generating every spoken word. The representation may emphasize events, semantics, or captions instead of exact linguistic content. Pair quality, negative sampling, dataset shortcuts, and prompt phrasing affect behavior. Evaluate with realistic queries and candidate sets, and separately measure transcription if that is required; one benchmark does not establish both capabilities.

The embedding may rely on session or channel characteristics correlated with speaker or text labels rather than the desired identity or semantics. Split by speaker, session, source recording, device, or environment according to the generalization claim, and prevent near-duplicate segments from crossing splits. Inspect genuine/impostor or retrieval scores across conditions and use targeted augmentation or adaptation when appropriate. Randomly splitting short clips from the same original recording can make held-out performance look stronger than deployment behavior.

questions: What decisions must a text-to-speech system make beyond mapping written characters to acoustic frames?
A TTS model skips words or repeats phrases even though its training loss decreases. What alignment and data issues would you examine?

A duration model allocates [2,3,1,4] frames to four linguistic units with a 10-millisecond hop. What total duration is predicted, and what should be checked before interpreting these as exact waveform boundaries?
Compare autoregressive generation, parallel prediction, and iterative refinement for speech quality, dependency modeling, and latency.
An iterative generator uses 30 sequential refinement steps taking 15 milliseconds each. What is the refinement-only latency, and why is that not its full time to first playable audio?
How does a neural vocoder differ from a neural audio codec? Why are Mel features not directly playable audio?
A codec emits eight codebook indices per frame at 75 frames/second, with 1,024 choices per index. Ignoring entropy coding and metadata, compute its bitrate.
A conditioned speech generator preserves the words but drifts away from the requested speaker identity during long output. Which dimensions should be evaluated separately?
Why can a pointwise acoustic reconstruction objective favor an unconvincing average when several speech realizations are valid?
A speech-to-speech system’s text content is correct, but playback contains discontinuities at chunk boundaries. What would you inspect before retraining its language model?
answers: It must interpret text normalization and pronunciation, align linguistic units with durations, and choose prosody such as stress, pitch, rhythm, and pauses. The same words can have multiple valid realizations depending on context and speaking style. An acoustic representation then needs a compatible waveform generation stage. Separate intelligibility, pronunciation, speaker similarity, naturalness, controllability, and latency in evaluation. A lower reconstruction loss alone does not establish that all these user-visible properties improved.

Inspect text/audio pairing, normalization, tokenization, length masks, attention or duration alignment, and difficult sequence lengths. A monotonic or explicit-duration mechanism can help when the task’s temporal order supports it, but cannot fix wrong transcripts. Autoregressive inference can also visit histories different from teacher-forced training. Listen to targeted examples and compare word coverage as well as acoustic loss. Distinguish an alignment or generation-loop failure from a vocoder artifact before changing the entire model.

The durations sum to 10 frames, corresponding to 100 milliseconds on the stated frame grid. This is an acoustic-frame duration convention, not automatically exact sample-boundary timing for every frontend or synthesis system. Check padding, centering, frame definitions, and the vocoder’s upsampling and context requirements. Duration changes also alter speaking rate and perceived prosody, so a numerical alignment fit should be assessed together with intelligibility and naturalness rather than treated as the sole objective.

Autoregressive generation conditions on preceding outputs but introduces sequential steps and possible accumulated inference errors. Parallel prediction can generate many positions at once, often relying on explicit durations or other structural assumptions, and may underrepresent variability if the objective favors a mean output. Iterative refinement can model rich distributions but spends repeated computation improving a candidate. Actual latency also depends on context, chunking, kernels, and waveform generation. Compare matched quality and end-to-end delay rather than ordering these families by name alone.

The refinement computation takes 30 × 15 = 450 milliseconds under the stated sequential timing. First playable audio can also require text/frontend preparation, enough model context, buffering, acoustic decoding or a vocoder, scheduling, and transfer to playback. Chunked generation may alter which stages can overlap, but it needs a supported causal or bounded-context design. Reducing refinement steps can change quality, so validate both the latency and output distribution instead of claiming a free speedup.

A vocoder synthesizes a waveform from an acoustic representation such as a Mel spectrogram, which typically lacks phase and fine spectral information needed for unique inversion. A codec encodes and decodes audio using a compressed representation, often quantized latent codes with a defined bitrate and reconstruction tradeoff. A speech-language system can use codec tokens as generative units, but token generation and waveform decoding remain distinct stages. Match representation conventions and evaluate perceptual fidelity, intelligibility, delay, and storage or transmission cost.

Each index requires log₂(1024) = 10 bits. Eight indices at 75 frames per second therefore require 8 × 75 × 10 = 6,000 bits/second, or 6 kilobits/second in decimal units. There are 600 indices per second, which is a different unit from frames or bits. Metadata, packetization, entropy coding, and any additional streams change actual bitrate. Lower payload rate does not by itself guarantee lower generation latency, since the model may still predict indices sequentially or need future context.

Measure linguistic correctness, identity similarity, prosody, naturalness, and stability over time rather than reducing the result to transcript accuracy. Inspect conditioning strength, training coverage, long-horizon generation behavior, codec/acoustic representation, and the compatibility of enrollment or prompt audio. A model can preserve semantics while losing identity or acoustic continuity. Use held-out speakers and realistic prompt lengths with appropriate task-specific evaluation; a text-based score cannot establish the requested voice characteristics.

One text can legitimately correspond to different durations, pitch contours, emphasis, and fine waveform details. A deterministic mean-oriented objective can average incompatible realizations into a representation that is numerically close to references but sounds oversmoothed or unnatural. Explicit conditioning or a probabilistic generative objective can represent variation, with added modeling and evaluation requirements. Do not infer better naturalness solely from lower reconstruction error; assess intelligibility, perceptual quality, and intended variation using a consistent protocol.

Check acoustic/codec frame alignment, retained decoder state, overlap or cross-fade conventions, vocoder context, sample-rate handling, and whether adjacent chunks use consistent conditioning. A generation or synthesis boundary can create audible artifacts even when the linguistic sequence is correct. Trace the intermediate representations and compare offline versus chunked reconstruction to localize the first discontinuity. End-to-end evaluation should include playback continuity and latency, rather than treating the text component as the explanation for every audio defect.

questions: How would you establish a useful baseline and train/test split for a speech model expected to work on unseen speakers and recording sessions?
Clean-speech validation is strong, but the deployed recognizer fails on accents and background noise. What data and error analyses would guide adaptation?
A reference contains ten words. Recognition makes one substitution, two deletions, and one insertion. Compute WER. Why can the same rate have different user impact across tasks?
One utterance has two reference words and one error; another has eight reference words and one error. Compare corpus WER with the unweighted mean of utterance WERs.
Processing two seconds of audio takes 1.5 seconds. What is the real-time factor, and why does a value below one not prove low interactive latency?
A recognizer’s kernels are fast, but final transcripts appear half a second after the user stops. How would you separate endpointing delay from encoder lookahead and scheduling?
When would quantization, batching, caching, or a smaller model help audio deployment, and what should be revalidated?
Outline the measurable stages of an end-to-end streaming speech service from microphone input to final output.
Aggregate WER improves after a release, but command success falls for one device family. What evidence should trigger a rollback or targeted correction?
How would you compare an accurate offline model with a slightly less accurate streaming model for an interactive voice task?
answers: Define the output, deployment channel, relevant languages and conditions, and a task-specific quality/latency target. Compare a simple or pretrained baseline using the exact frontend and scoring rules. Split at the speaker/session/source-recording level needed for the generalization claim, avoiding duplicate or near-duplicate segments across partitions. Reserve independent test conditions after tuning. A random split of clips is insufficient if it lets a model recognize recording-specific or speaker-specific shortcuts that will not transfer.

Break down errors by accent, language, device, noise condition, utterance length, and relevant user task while checking sample sizes. Inspect recordings and label conventions, frontend mismatch, and whether the training distribution covers those slices. Consider representative noise/reverberation augmentation, balanced sampling, additional labels, or adaptation from the baseline. Test that augmentations preserve the target. Track overall and slice metrics on held-out conditions so improved robustness in one group does not silently mask regressions in another.

Word error rate is (substitutions + deletions + insertions)/reference words = (1 + 2 + 1)/10 = 40%. It counts aligned word edits, not the percentage of predicted words that are wrong. A missed contact name, negation, or command keyword can matter more than a formatting variation in some applications. Keep normalization and tokenization conventions fixed, inspect error types and important entities, and supplement aggregate WER with task completion or targeted metrics where the product objective requires them.

Corpus WER aggregates edits and reference counts: (1 + 1)/(2 + 8) = 20%. The unweighted utterance mean is (50% + 12.5%)/2 = 31.25%. They answer different weighting questions, giving equal weight to words or to utterances. Report the chosen convention explicitly and use consistent normalization. Slice and user-level metrics can still be valuable, but they should not be substituted silently for the corpus metric when comparing recognition systems.

The real-time factor is compute time divided by audio duration, 1.5/2 = 0.75. That indicates faster-than-real-time processing for the measured workload, not necessarily immediate outputs. The system can still wait for a full utterance, future context, chunk assembly, batching, or endpoint detection before emitting stable text. Measure partial-output timing, finalization delay after speech ends, queueing, and tail behavior under realistic concurrent streams. State whether timing includes frontend, decoding, and transfer overhead.

Timestamp audio arrival, frontend frames, encoder readiness, hypothesis updates, endpoint decisions, and final output. Lookahead waits for future acoustic context; endpointing waits for evidence that speech has ended; batching and queues delay ready work. Reducing one component may leave another as the bottleneck. Compare accuracy and premature-cutoff rates when tuning endpointing, and evaluate real chunk arrivals instead of feeding the complete recording as quickly as possible. Low average kernel duration is not a full latency measurement.

Choose from the measured bottleneck: quantization can reduce model storage or arithmetic cost, batching can improve utilization while adding waiting, and caching can reuse valid state across streaming chunks. A smaller model may lower compute but reduce quality on difficult conditions. Check supported kernels, memory, state lifetimes, channel/frontend consistency, and per-stream latency at representative load. Revalidate recognition or task quality, especially important slices, rather than assuming compressed weights or higher throughput preserve every operating characteristic.

Specify capture and sample-rate/channel handling, causal or bounded-lookahead features, model context and state, decoding or task decisions, endpointing, and output delivery. For each stage define ownership, timing, masks, and reset behavior. Choose metrics for quality, false triggers or word errors as appropriate, latency, capacity, and resource use. Establish a baseline, evaluate representative data and hard slices, and monitor the same interface conventions after deployment. This connects model decisions to the audio and product constraints they must actually satisfy.

Inspect per-device data volume and confidence, audio/frontend changes, important-word errors, recognition-to-command mapping, latency, and endpoint behavior. The aggregate gain may come from a larger easy population while the affected group regresses, or the command metric may reveal costs WER weights poorly. Compare with the previous version under matched conditions and reproduce representative failures. Use defined quality and service criteria for rollback or correction, and monitor independent outcomes rather than relying only on the training or aggregate optimization metric.

Use the real interaction objective: quality on relevant utterances, first and final response timing, premature endpointing, corrections, resource limits, and concurrent demand. An offline model may rely on future audio or long batches that violate the task even with better WER. A streaming model must be trained and evaluated with its actual context constraints. Compare task success and latency distributions at supported load, including difficult acoustic slices, rather than declaring a winner from one offline score.
